This notebook expands the third unit of the course. The lecture slides are a map; this text is the territory. Unit 2 introduced learning from data and a first classifier, logistic regression, which draws a straight boundary through feature space. This unit presents three further families of classifiers that approach the same problem from three different directions: probabilistic methods, which model how the data of each class are generated and then invert the model with Bayes' theorem (naive Bayes, Bayesian networks); geometric methods, which search directly for the boundary with the largest margin of safety (support vector machines); and memory-based methods, which store the training sample and classify by analogy with the nearest stored cases (k-nearest neighbours). Every method is first derived, then implemented by hand in a few lines of numpy, then compared with the scikit-learn implementation, and finally exercised on the breast-cancer data that recur throughout the course. Section 8 compares the three families honestly, with the methodology of Supplement S1.

Learning objectives

  • State Bayes' theorem, apply it by hand to a diagnostic test, and explain why a positive result of an accurate test for a rare disease is usually a false positive.
  • Define the posterior probability, the Bayes classifier and the Bayes error, and show how unequal misclassification costs move the decision threshold.
  • Derive the Gaussian naive Bayes classifier from the conditional-independence assumption, implement it with numpy, and explain why it classifies well even when the assumption is false.
  • Read a Bayesian network as a factorisation of a joint distribution, perform inference by enumeration on a small medical network, and explain how evidence and d-separation change posteriors.
  • Describe the k-nearest-neighbours rule, its distance metrics, its dependence on feature scaling and on k, its computational cost, and the curse of dimensionality.
  • Explain the maximum-margin principle, the roles of support vectors, the parameter C and the kernel, and the relation between the hinge loss and the logistic loss of Unit 2.
  • Compare the three families on the same data with stratified cross-validation and choose among them from their assumptions, costs and interpretability.

How to read this notebook

Each code cell is short and commented. Run it, read its output, then read the paragraph that interprets the output. Exercises (green boxes) ask you to modify the cell above them and re-run; they are the fastest way to learn. Blue boxes carry key ideas, orange boxes carry common misconceptions, and purple boxes connect this unit to other units or to the bioinformatics course (BGM324). The notebook uses only numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy and scikit-learn, all pre-installed in Google Colab; no data is downloaded. Four algorithms are traced by hand on paper-sized examples (Sections 2.2, 4.2, 4.3 and 6.1) before the code confirms them. Evaluation methodology — why cases are held out, what cross-validation is, what the AUC measures — is assumed from Supplement S1 and not re-derived here.

# Setup: libraries used throughout the notebook. Random seeds are fixed so that every
# number quoted in the text is reproducible.
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, scipy, sklearn
from sklearn import datasets

np.random.seed(0)
pd.set_option("display.width", 130); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 100, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
                     "font.size": 9, "axes.titlesize": 10, "axes.titleweight": "bold"})
BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, GREY = "#2b5d9b", "#d2691e", "#3a7d44", "#7f7f7f"   # benign, malignant, accent, neutral
print("numpy", np.__version__, "| pandas", pd.__version__, "| scipy", scipy.__version__, "| scikit-learn", sklearn.__version__)

numpy 2.4.6 | pandas 3.0.3 | scipy 1.17.1 | scikit-learn 1.9.0

1. Three ways to draw a boundary

Unit 1 defined a classifier as a rule that partitions feature space into regions and assigns a class to each, and Unit 2 built the first such rule, logistic regression, whose regions are separated by a straight line. There are many ways to arrive at a boundary, and the methods of this unit represent three of them.

  1. Probabilistic (generative) methods ask how the data of each class are distributed — "what do the features of malignant tumours look like, and of benign ones?" — estimate those distributions from the training sample, and then use Bayes' theorem to turn them into the probability of each class given the features. The boundary is the set of points where two classes are equally probable. Naive Bayes (Section 4) and Bayesian networks (Section 5) belong here.
  2. Geometric (discriminative) methods do not model the classes at all. They search directly for the boundary that separates the training cases, and among all boundaries that do so, they choose the one that leaves the widest empty corridor — the margin — between the classes. The support vector machine (Section 7) is the canonical example. Logistic regression is also discriminative, but it chooses its line by a different criterion.
  3. Memory-based (instance-based) methods build no model and no explicit boundary. They store the training sample and, when a new case arrives, look up the most similar stored cases and copy their label. The k-nearest-neighbours rule (Section 6) is the archetype; its boundary exists only implicitly, as the places where the majority among the neighbours changes.

The distinction matters because the three families fail differently. A generative model is only as good as its assumptions about the class distributions; a margin-based model is only as good as its choice of boundary shape; a memory-based model is only as good as its notion of similarity and the density of stored cases. The same two-feature problem will be solved by all three so that the differences can be seen. The data are, as in every unit, the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer sample: 569 fine-needle aspirates described by 30 nuclear features and labelled by biopsy.[4] For the two-dimensional pictures we keep the two features used by hand in Unit 1, mean radius and mean concave points (the latter multiplied by 100 to bring the two ranges closer together); the full 30-feature problem returns in Section 8.

# The recurring example: two features of the breast-cancer data, split once into training (70 %) and test (30 %).
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
cancer = datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X, y = cancer.data, cancer.target                         # y: 0 = malignant, 1 = benign (scikit-learn's coding)
X2 = X[["mean radius", "mean concave points"]].to_numpy() * np.array([1, 100])
X2_tr, X2_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X2, y.to_numpy(), test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
print(f"training cases: {len(y_tr)} (malignant {np.sum(y_tr == 0)}, benign {np.sum(y_tr == 1)}) | test cases: {len(y_te)}")

def plot_regions(ax, clf, Xp, yp, title, xlim=(6, 30), ylim=(-1, 22), res=250):
    '''Shade the decision regions of a fitted 2-feature classifier and draw the points on top.'''
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(*xlim, res), np.linspace(*ylim, res))
    Z = clf.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"], alpha=0.9)
    for c, col, name in [(0, ORANGE, "malignant"), (1, BLUE, "benign")]:
        ax.scatter(*Xp[yp == c].T, color=col, s=10, edgecolor="none", label=name)
    ax.set_xlim(*xlim); ax.set_ylim(*ylim); ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("mean radius (µm)"); ax.set_ylabel("mean concave points × 100")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4))
for c, col, name in [(0, ORANGE, "malignant"), (1, BLUE, "benign")]:
    ax.scatter(*X2_tr[y_tr == c].T, color=col, s=12, edgecolor="none", label=f"{name} (training)")
ax.set_xlabel("mean radius (µm)"); ax.set_ylabel("mean concave points × 100"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title("The two-feature problem that all three families will solve"); fig.tight_layout()

training cases: 398 (malignant 148, benign 250) | test cases: 171

Figure 1. The 398 training cases in the plane of mean radius and mean concave points. The classes are separable in the bulk but overlap in a band of intermediate values; no boundary of any shape will classify every case correctly, and the question for every method is where, and with what shape, to draw the line through the overlap.

The cell below shows the answer each of the three families gives, with default settings, before any of them has been explained. The figure is a preview to return to: by the end of the unit every feature of the three panels — the curved boundary of naive Bayes, the straight band of the linear support vector machine, the jagged islands of k-nearest neighbours — will have an explanation.

# Preview: the same problem solved by a probabilistic, a geometric and a memory-based classifier.
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
previews = [("Probabilistic:\nGaussian naive Bayes", GaussianNB()),
            ("Geometric:\nlinear SVM", SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0)),
            ("Memory-based:\n5 nearest neighbours", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.3), sharey=True)
for ax, (title, clf) in zip(axes, previews):
    clf.fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
    plot_regions(ax, clf, X2_te, y_te, f"{title}\ntest accuracy {clf.score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}")
    if ax is not axes[0]: ax.set_ylabel("")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 2. Decision regions of the three families on the 171 test cases, each fitted with scikit-learn defaults to the 398 training cases. The accuracies in the titles are all close to 0.9 — the problem is easy enough that any sensible rule does well — but the boundaries differ in shape: naive Bayes draws a smooth curve (a conic section, Section 4.4), the linear support vector machine a straight line placed to maximise the gap between the classes (Section 7.1), and k-nearest neighbours an irregular frontier that follows the local majority (Section 6.4). The differences are invisible in the accuracy and decisive in how each method behaves away from the data.

2. The probability needed for this unit

Two of the three families are built on probability, and the third is best understood through it (Section 6.2). This section reviews only the three facts that are needed, and introduces the running diagnostic example that will be solved by hand.

2.1 Joint, marginal and conditional probability

For two events $A$ and $B$ — say $D$, "the patient has the disease", and $T$, "the test is positive" — the joint probability $P(D, T)$ is the probability that both occur; the marginal probability $P(T)$ is the probability of $T$ regardless of $D$, obtained by summing the joint over the possibilities for $D$ (the law of total probability, $P(T) = P(T, D) + P(T, \neg D)$); and the conditional probability $P(T \mid D)$ is the probability of $T$ among the cases where $D$ holds, defined by

$$P(T \mid D) = \frac{P(T, D)}{P(D)} \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad P(T, D) = P(T \mid D)\, P(D).$$

The second form is the product rule, and it is symmetric: $P(T, D) = P(D \mid T)\, P(T)$ as well. Two events are independent when $P(T \mid D) = P(T)$, i.e. when knowing one tells nothing about the other, in which case the joint factorises as $P(T, D) = P(T)\,P(D)$. Two events are conditionally independent given a third, $C$, when $P(A, B \mid C) = P(A \mid C)\, P(B \mid C)$: within each value of $C$ they carry no information about each other, although they may be strongly associated overall. This last notion is the foundation of both naive Bayes and Bayesian networks.

2.2 Bayes' theorem, by hand

Equating the two forms of the product rule and dividing by $P(T)$ gives the result that Thomas Bayes left in a manuscript published posthumously in 1763:[1]

$$P(D \mid T) = \frac{P(T \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(T)} = \frac{P(T \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(T \mid D)\, P(D) + P(T \mid \neg D)\, P(\neg D)}$$ where $P(D)$ is the prior probability of the disease before the test (in a screening setting, the prevalence), $P(T \mid D)$ is the likelihood of the observed result under the disease (for a positive test, the sensitivity), $P(T)$ is the evidence or marginal probability of the observed result, and $P(D \mid T)$ is the posterior probability of the disease after the test — in clinical language, the positive predictive value (PPV).

The theorem is an identity; its content lies in the direction of the inference. Test characteristics are measured in the forward direction (how does the test behave in people known to be ill?), whereas the clinician needs the backward direction (how likely is illness in a person whose test is positive?). The two directions are related only through the prior, and the neglect of the prior — base-rate neglect — is a well-documented error: when Casscells and colleagues asked staff and students at Harvard Medical School a version of the problem below, fewer than one in five gave the right answer, and the most common answer was off by a factor of five.[2]

Worked example. A screening test for a disease with prevalence 1 % has sensitivity 95 % ($P(T \mid D) = 0.95$) and specificity 95 % ($P(\neg T \mid \neg D) = 0.95$, so the false-positive rate is $P(T \mid \neg D) = 0.05$). A person tests positive. What is the probability that they have the disease?

$$P(D \mid T) = \frac{0.95 \times 0.01}{0.95 \times 0.01 + 0.05 \times 0.99} = \frac{0.0095}{0.0095 + 0.0495} = \frac{0.0095}{0.0590} \approx 0.161.$$

A positive result from a test that is right 95 % of the time in both directions leaves the patient with only a 16 % probability of disease, because the 1 % of true cases who test positive (0.95 × 1 % ≈ 0.95 % of everyone) are outnumbered five to one by the 99 % of healthy people who test falsely positive (0.05 × 99 % ≈ 4.95 % of everyone). The same arithmetic is far easier to follow in natural frequencies — counts in a notional population of 10,000 — than in probabilities, as Gigerenzer and Hoffrage showed experimentally,[3] and the cell below lays it out both ways.

# Bayes' theorem on the screening example, as probabilities and as natural frequencies in 10,000 people.
prevalence, sensitivity, specificity = 0.01, 0.95, 0.95
p_pos_given_D, p_pos_given_notD = sensitivity, 1 - specificity
evidence = p_pos_given_D * prevalence + p_pos_given_notD * (1 - prevalence)      # P(T) by total probability
ppv = p_pos_given_D * prevalence / evidence
print(f"P(T) = {evidence:.4f}   P(D | T) = PPV = {ppv:.4f}")

N = 10_000
ill, healthy = N * prevalence, N * (1 - prevalence)
freq = pd.DataFrame({"test positive": [ill * sensitivity, healthy * (1 - specificity)],
                     "test negative": [ill * (1 - sensitivity), healthy * specificity]},
                    index=["ill (100)", "healthy (9,900)"]).astype(int)
freq["total"] = freq.sum(axis=1)
print(f"Of the {freq['test positive'].sum()} positives, {freq.loc['ill (100)', 'test positive']} are ill: "
      f"{freq.loc['ill (100)', 'test positive'] / freq['test positive'].sum():.3f}")
print(freq.to_string())

# Positive predictive value as a function of prevalence, for three specificities (sensitivity fixed at 0.95).
prev = np.linspace(0.001, 0.6, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
for spec, col in [(0.95, BLUE), (0.99, GREEN), (0.999, ORANGE)]:
    ax.plot(prev * 100, 0.95 * prev / (0.95 * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev)), color=col, label=f"specificity {spec}")
ax.axvline(1, color=GREY, ls=":", lw=1); ax.plot(1, ppv, "o", color=BLUE)
ax.annotate(f"prevalence 1 %, PPV {ppv:.2f}", (1, ppv), xytext=(6, 0.12), fontsize=8,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=GREY))
ax.set_xlabel("prevalence (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("P(disease | positive test)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.legend(frameon=False); ax.set_title("The posterior depends on the prior: PPV vs prevalence"); fig.tight_layout()
for p in [0.01, 0.10, 0.30]:
    print(f"prevalence {p:.0%}: PPV = {0.95 * p / (0.95 * p + 0.05 * (1 - p)):.3f} (specificity 0.95)")

P(T) = 0.0590   P(D | T) = PPV = 0.1610
Of the 590 positives, 95 are ill: 0.161
                 test positive  test negative  total
ill (100)                   95              5    100
healthy (9,900)            495           9405   9900
prevalence 1%: PPV = 0.161 (specificity 0.95)
prevalence 10%: PPV = 0.679 (specificity 0.95)
prevalence 30%: PPV = 0.891 (specificity 0.95)

The code reproduces the hand calculation: the PPV is 0.161. In the frequency table, 95 of the 100 ill people and 495 of the 9,900 healthy people test positive, so 95 of 590 positives are ill. The same test applied in a hospital ward where the prevalence is 30 % rather than 1 % would behave very differently; the figure traces the PPV over the whole range of prevalence and also shows what a more specific test buys.

Figure 3. Positive predictive value against prevalence for a test with sensitivity 0.95 and three specificities. At 1 % prevalence the 95 %-specific test yields a PPV of 0.16; at 10 % it yields about 0.68 and at 30 % about 0.89 (printed values). Raising the specificity to 0.999 makes the test useful even in screening. The lesson transfers directly to classifiers: a model's sensitivity and specificity are properties of the model, but the meaning of its positive output depends on the population it is applied to, which is one reason why the external-validation failures of Unit 1 happened in hospitals with a different case mix.

Common misconception

"The test is 95 % accurate, so a positive result means a 95 % chance of disease." The 95 % is $P(T \mid D)$; the clinician needs $P(D \mid T)$. The two are equal only when the prior is 50 %. Every probabilistic classifier in this unit outputs a posterior, and every posterior inherits the prior that was built into it — by the class proportions of the training sample. A naive Bayes model trained on a sample that is half malignant will overstate the probability of malignancy in a screening population; Section 3.1 shows where the prior enters.

2.3 Bayes' theorem for classification

Replacing the binary event $D$ with a class label $y \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ and the test result with a feature vector $\mathbf{x}$ gives the form used throughout this unit:

$$P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)\, P(y = c)}{p(\mathbf{x})} = \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)\, P(y = c)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = k)\, P(y = k)}.$$

The lower-case $p$ marks a probability density, because features are usually continuous: $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)$ is the class-conditional density — the distribution of the features among the cases of class $c$ — and $P(y = c)$ is the class prior. A generative classifier is a recipe for estimating these two objects from the training sample; once they are in hand, the posterior follows from the formula, and the denominator can be ignored when comparing classes because it is the same for all of them.

3. Bayesian decision theory

3.1 The Bayes classifier and the Bayes error

Suppose for a moment that the class-conditional densities and the priors are known exactly. Then the posterior $P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x})$ is known for every $\mathbf{x}$, and the rule that assigns each $\mathbf{x}$ to the class of highest posterior,

$$\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\max_c \, P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) = \arg\max_c \, p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)\, P(y = c),$$

is the Bayes classifier. It is optimal in a precise sense: no other rule has a lower probability of error. Its error, the Bayes error, is the irreducible error of the problem — the part caused by genuine overlap of the classes in feature space, which no amount of data or modelling can remove. Where the two classes have equal posterior, $P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) = 1/2$ in the binary case, is the Bayes decision boundary; every classifier in this course can be read as an attempt to approximate it from a finite sample. The prior enters as a multiplicative weight on each class: doubling the prior of malignancy doubles its posterior odds everywhere, and moves the boundary toward the benign side.

3.2 Minimum-error and minimum-risk decisions

Choosing the most probable class minimises the number of errors. In medicine the two kinds of error rarely cost the same: a malignant tumour called benign is a missed cancer, a benign one called malignant is an unnecessary biopsy. Let $\lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}$ be the cost of a false negative (deciding benign when the truth is malignant) and $\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}}$ the cost of a false positive. The expected risk of each decision at a point $\mathbf{x}$ is

$$R(\text{decide benign} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}\, P(M \mid \mathbf{x}), \qquad R(\text{decide malignant} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \lambda_{\mathrm{FP}}\, P(B \mid \mathbf{x}),$$

and the minimum-risk rule decides malignant when the first exceeds the second, i.e. when

$$P(M \mid \mathbf{x}) > \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}}.$$

With equal costs the threshold is $1/2$ and the rule reduces to the minimum-error rule. If a missed cancer is judged five times as costly as an unnecessary biopsy, the threshold falls to $1/6 \approx 0.167$: the classifier calls a case malignant as soon as the posterior exceeds one sixth. The cell below builds the whole machinery on a single feature, mean radius, by fitting one Gaussian per class and using the class proportions of the training sample as priors.

# Bayesian decision theory in one dimension: Gaussian class-conditionals of 'mean radius', priors, posterior, thresholds.
from scipy.stats import norm
r_tr, r_te = X2_tr[:, 0], X2_te[:, 0]
prior = {c: np.mean(y_tr == c) for c in (0, 1)}                                 # class proportions in training
mu = {c: r_tr[y_tr == c].mean() for c in (0, 1)}; sd = {c: r_tr[y_tr == c].std() for c in (0, 1)}
grid = np.linspace(6, 30, 1000)
joint = {c: norm.pdf(grid, mu[c], sd[c]) * prior[c] for c in (0, 1)}            # p(x | c) P(c)
post_M = joint[0] / (joint[0] + joint[1])                                       # P(malignant | x)
t_err = grid[np.argmin(np.abs(post_M - 0.5))]                                   # minimum-error threshold
t_risk = grid[np.argmin(np.abs(post_M - 1 / 6))]                                # minimum-risk, FN costs 5x FP
print(f"priors: malignant {prior[0]:.3f}, benign {prior[1]:.3f} | means: {mu[0]:.2f} vs {mu[1]:.2f} µm, sd: {sd[0]:.2f} vs {sd[1]:.2f}")
print(f"radius threshold: minimum-error {t_err:.2f} µm | minimum-risk (missed cancer 5x costlier) {t_risk:.2f} µm")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
axes[0].plot(grid, joint[0], color=ORANGE, label="p(x | malignant) P(malignant)")
axes[0].plot(grid, joint[1], color=BLUE, label="p(x | benign) P(benign)")
axes[0].fill_between(grid, 0, np.minimum(joint[0], joint[1]), color=GREY, alpha=0.35, label="Bayes error (overlap)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("mean radius (µm)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("density × prior"); axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5)
axes[0].set_title("Class-conditional densities weighted by the priors")
axes[1].plot(grid, post_M, color=ORANGE); axes[1].set_xlabel("mean radius (µm)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("P(malignant | x)")
for t, lev, lab, col in [(t_err, 0.5, "equal costs", "k"), (t_risk, 1 / 6, "FN costs 5× FP", GREEN)]:
    axes[1].axhline(lev, color=col, ls=":", lw=1); axes[1].axvline(t, color=col, ls="--", lw=1, label=f"{lab}: {t:.1f} µm")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); axes[1].set_title("Posterior and the two decision thresholds"); fig.tight_layout()

# Consequences of the two rules on the 171 test cases: errors of each kind and total cost (FN = 5, FP = 1).
rows = []
for name, t in [("minimum error (threshold 1/2)", t_err), ("minimum risk (threshold 1/6)", t_risk)]:
    call_M = r_te >= t                                    # larger radius -> call malignant; smaller -> benign
    FN = np.sum(~call_M & (y_te == 0)); FP = np.sum(call_M & (y_te == 1))
    rows.append({"rule": name, "false negatives": FN, "false positives": FP, "errors": FN + FP,
                 "sensitivity": np.mean(call_M[y_te == 0]).round(3), "specificity": np.mean(~call_M[y_te == 1]).round(3),
                 "total cost (5·FN + FP)": 5 * FN + FP})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("rule").to_string())

minimum risk (threshold 1/6)                 8               30      38        0.875        0.720                      70

Figure 4. Left: the two class-conditional Gaussians of mean radius, each multiplied by its prior, so that the curves are proportional to the posterior; the shaded overlap is the region in which the Bayes classifier must err. Right: the posterior probability of malignancy. The equal-cost threshold is where the posterior crosses 0.5 (about 15 µm); when a missed cancer is five times as costly as an unnecessary biopsy, the threshold moves to where the posterior crosses 1/6 (about 13.5 µm), and more cases are called malignant. The small rise of the posterior at very small radii is a real property of the two-Gaussian model, not an error: the malignant Gaussian is wider, so far from both means its tails exceed the benign density — the same variance effect that decides the hand example of Section 4.3; in practice one would not call a 7 µm nucleus malignant, which is a reminder that a model is only trustworthy where there are data.

The two thresholds trade one kind of error for the other. The table printed above the figure applies both to the 171 test cases and counts the consequences, including the total cost under the 5 : 1 assumption.

The minimum-error rule makes fewer errors in total; the minimum-risk rule makes more errors but fewer of the expensive kind, and its total cost under the stated costs is lower. Neither rule is "better" in the abstract: the choice of costs is a clinical and ethical decision that the engineer must elicit and make explicit, not a modelling detail. Supplement S1 generalises this trade-off into the ROC curve, which displays all thresholds at once.

Key idea

Bayesian decision theory separates two things that are often confused: estimating the posterior probability of each class, which is a statistical problem, and deciding what to do with it, which depends on the costs of the possible errors. A classifier that outputs calibrated probabilities can serve any cost structure by moving the threshold; one that outputs only labels has baked in the assumption of equal costs.

4. Naive Bayes

4.1 The conditional-independence assumption

To use Bayes' theorem for classification one must estimate the class-conditional density $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)$. For a single feature this is easy: a histogram or a fitted Gaussian will do. For $p = 30$ features it is hopeless in general, because a joint density over 30 dimensions has far too many degrees of freedom to be estimated from a few hundred cases — the curse of dimensionality that Section 6.5 will quantify. The naive Bayes classifier escapes by assuming that, within each class, the features are independent of one another:

$$p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c) = \prod_{j=1}^{p} p(x_j \mid y = c), \qquad\text{so that}\qquad P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto P(y = c) \prod_{j=1}^{p} p(x_j \mid y = c).$$ The 30-dimensional density is replaced by 30 one-dimensional densities per class, each of which can be estimated from the data of that class alone. The classifier then needs only the per-class prior and, for each feature, a one-dimensional model of its distribution in each class.

The assumption is almost always false — in the breast-cancer data, radius, perimeter and area of the same nucleus are nearly perfectly correlated within each class — which is why the method is called naive, or in Hand and Yu's phrase, "idiot's Bayes".[6] Section 4.6 explains why it works anyway. In practice the product is computed as a sum of logarithms, because the product of thirty densities underflows the floating-point range:

$$\log P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) = \log P(y = c) + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \log p(x_j \mid y = c) + \text{const}.$$

The choice of the one-dimensional model $p(x_j \mid y = c)$ gives the variants of the method. Gaussian naive Bayes, for continuous features, fits a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{cj}, \sigma^2_{cj})$ to each feature in each class, so training consists of computing a mean and a variance per feature and class, plus the class proportions. Multinomial naive Bayes, for count features such as word frequencies in a document, models each class by a probability vector over the vocabulary; Bernoulli naive Bayes, for binary features (word present or absent), models each feature by a per-class probability of being 1. The last two are the classical spam filter and the baseline of text classification, including the classification of clinical notes; Section 4.7 shows one of them on image data.

Naive Bayes has three practical virtues that the lecture slides summarise and that the rest of this section will bear out: it is easy to build (no iterative optimisation, no hyper-parameters beyond a smoothing constant), it is efficient (training is a single pass over the data, prediction is a sum of $p$ terms), and it performs well on very large and high-dimensional data, including noisy data, because the number of parameters grows only linearly with the number of features.

4.2 Naive Bayes by hand: the weather example

The classical hand example, used in the lecture slides and in most textbooks, is Quinlan's fourteen-day "play tennis" dataset: four categorical features — Outlook (Sunny / Overcast / Rainy), Temperature (Hot / Mild / Cool), Humidity (High / Normal) and Windy (True / False) — and a binary target, whether the match was played (Yes on 9 days, No on 5).[12] The computation has three steps.

Step 1 — frequency table. Count, for each value of Outlook, how many days fell in each class:

Outlook No Yes total
Overcast 0 4 4
Rainy 3 2 5
Sunny 2 3 5
total 5 9 14

Step 2 — likelihood table. Convert the counts to probabilities: the prior $P(\text{Yes}) = 9/14 = 0.64$, the evidence $P(\text{Sunny}) = 5/14 = 0.36$, and the likelihood $P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Yes}) = 3/9 = 0.33$.

Step 3 — posterior. Bayes' theorem gives $P(\text{Yes} \mid \text{Sunny}) = \dfrac{P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Yes})\, P(\text{Yes})}{P(\text{Sunny})} = \dfrac{0.33 \times 0.64}{0.36} = 0.60$, so on a sunny day the prediction is play. (Exactly, $\tfrac{3}{9} \cdot \tfrac{9}{14} \big/ \tfrac{5}{14} = 3/5$.)

With all four features the "naive" step enters: the likelihood of the whole day is the product of the per-feature likelihoods. The conditional tables for every feature value are, as fractions of the 9 Yes-days and the 5 No-days:

Outlook Yes No Temperature Yes No Humidity Yes No Windy Yes No
Sunny 3/9 2/5 Hot 2/9 2/5 High 3/9 4/5 False 6/9 2/5
Overcast 4/9 0/5 Mild 4/9 2/5 Normal 6/9 1/5 True 3/9 3/5
Rainy 2/9 3/5 Cool 3/9 1/5

Query: Outlook = Rainy, Temperature = Mild, Humidity = Normal, Windy = True. The unnormalised posteriors are

$P(\text{Yes}) \prod_j P(x_j \mid \text{Yes}) = \tfrac{9}{14} \times \tfrac{2}{9} \times \tfrac{4}{9} \times \tfrac{6}{9} \times \tfrac{3}{9} = 0.6429 \times 0.2222 \times 0.4444 \times 0.6667 \times 0.3333 \approx 0.01411$

$P(\text{No}) \prod_j P(x_j \mid \text{No}) = \tfrac{5}{14} \times \tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{2}{5} \times \tfrac{1}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{5} = 0.3571 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.2 \times 0.6 \approx 0.01029$

and the normalisation divides each by their sum, $0.01411 + 0.01029 = 0.02440$ (which is $p(\mathbf{x})$, the evidence): $P(\text{Yes} \mid \mathbf{x}) = 0.01411 / 0.02440 \approx 0.578$ and $P(\text{No} \mid \mathbf{x}) = 0.01029 / 0.02440 \approx 0.422$. The prediction is play, with moderate confidence. Note the zero in the Overcast row of the No column: any overcast day would receive $P(\text{No} \mid \mathbf{x}) = 0$ regardless of the other three features, because a single zero annihilates the product. This is the zero-frequency problem, and the standard remedy, Laplace (additive) smoothing, adds a pseudo-count $\alpha$ to every cell before dividing: $P(x_j = v \mid c) = (n_{cv} + \alpha) / (n_c + \alpha\, m_j)$, where $m_j$ is the number of values of feature $j$. The cell below builds the fourteen days, repeats the computation with pandas, and then with scikit-learn's CategoricalNB, first without smoothing (reproducing the hand result) and then with $\alpha = 1$.

Where the slides differ from the original data

The frequency table above is the one in the lecture slides and in many online tutorials. In Quinlan's original table the Sunny and Rainy counts are the other way round (Sunny: 2 Yes, 3 No; Rainy: 3 Yes, 2 No),[12] so that the original answer for a sunny day is $P(\text{Yes} \mid \text{Sunny}) = 2/5 = 0.40$ — do not play. The arithmetic of the method is identical; only the labels of two outlook values are exchanged. The notebook follows the slides' table so that the numbers match the lecture; the dataset built below is Quinlan's with those two labels swapped.

# The fourteen-day weather dataset (as tabulated in the lecture slides), and naive Bayes computed with pandas.
weather = pd.DataFrame({
    "Outlook":     ["Rainy", "Rainy", "Overcast", "Sunny", "Sunny", "Sunny", "Overcast", "Rainy", "Rainy", "Sunny", "Rainy", "Overcast", "Overcast", "Sunny"],
    "Temperature": ["Hot", "Hot", "Hot", "Mild", "Cool", "Cool", "Cool", "Mild", "Cool", "Mild", "Mild", "Mild", "Hot", "Mild"],
    "Humidity":    ["High", "High", "High", "High", "Normal", "Normal", "Normal", "High", "Normal", "Normal", "Normal", "High", "Normal", "High"],
    "Windy":       [False, True, False, False, False, True, True, False, False, False, True, True, False, True],
    "Play":        ["No", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No"]})
print("Step 1 - frequency table for Outlook:"); print(pd.crosstab(weather["Outlook"], weather["Play"], margins=True).to_string(), "\n")
prior = weather["Play"].value_counts(normalize=True)                            # P(Yes), P(No)
def likelihood(feature, value, cls):
    '''P(feature = value | Play = cls) as a relative frequency among the days of that class.'''
    sub = weather[weather["Play"] == cls]
    return (sub[feature] == value).mean()
print(f"Step 2 - P(Sunny) = {(weather['Outlook'] == 'Sunny').mean():.2f}, P(Yes) = {prior['Yes']:.2f}, P(Sunny | Yes) = {likelihood('Outlook', 'Sunny', 'Yes'):.2f}")
print(f"Step 3 - P(Yes | Sunny) = {likelihood('Outlook', 'Sunny', 'Yes') * prior['Yes'] / (weather['Outlook'] == 'Sunny').mean():.2f}\n")
query_day = {"Outlook": "Rainy", "Temperature": "Mild", "Humidity": "Normal", "Windy": True}
unnorm = {c: prior[c] * np.prod([likelihood(f, v, c) for f, v in query_day.items()]) for c in ("Yes", "No")}
total = sum(unnorm.values())
print(f"Query {query_day}:")
for c in ("Yes", "No"):
    print(f"  P({c}) x product of likelihoods = {unnorm[c]:.5f}  ->  normalised P({c} | x) = {unnorm[c] / total:.3f}")

Step 1 - frequency table for Outlook:
Play      No  Yes  All
Outlook               
Overcast   0    4    4
Rainy      3    2    5
Sunny      2    3    5
All        5    9   14 

Step 2 - P(Sunny) = 0.36, P(Yes) = 0.64, P(Sunny | Yes) = 0.33
Step 3 - P(Yes | Sunny) = 0.60

Query {'Outlook': 'Rainy', 'Temperature': 'Mild', 'Humidity': 'Normal', 'Windy': True}:
  P(Yes) x product of likelihoods = 0.01411  ->  normalised P(Yes | x) = 0.578
  P(No) x product of likelihoods = 0.01029  ->  normalised P(No | x) = 0.422

# The same query with scikit-learn's CategoricalNB: alpha = 0 reproduces the hand result, alpha = 1 adds Laplace smoothing.
from sklearn.naive_bayes import CategoricalNB
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
features = ["Outlook", "Temperature", "Humidity", "Windy"]
enc = OrdinalEncoder().fit(weather[features].astype(str))
Xw = enc.transform(weather[features].astype(str)); yw = (weather["Play"] == "Yes").astype(int).to_numpy()
xq = enc.transform(pd.DataFrame([query_day])[features].astype(str))
import warnings
for alpha in (0, 1):
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")                     # alpha = 0 produces log(0) for the zero cell; expected
        cnb = CategoricalNB(alpha=alpha, force_alpha=True).fit(Xw, yw)
    p_yes = cnb.predict_proba(xq)[0, 1]
    print(f"alpha = {alpha}: P(Yes | Rainy, Mild, Normal, Windy) = {p_yes:.3f}")
# with alpha = 1 the likelihood of Rainy given Yes becomes (2 + 1) / (9 + 3) instead of 2 / 9:
print(f"P(Rainy | Yes): unsmoothed 2/9 = {2/9:.3f}; Laplace-smoothed (2+1)/(9+3) = {3/12:.3f}; "
      f"P(Overcast | No): unsmoothed 0/5 = 0, smoothed (0+1)/(5+3) = {1/8:.3f}")

alpha = 0: P(Yes | Rainy, Mild, Normal, Windy) = 0.578
alpha = 1: P(Yes | Rainy, Mild, Normal, Windy) = 0.586
P(Rainy | Yes): unsmoothed 2/9 = 0.222; Laplace-smoothed (2+1)/(9+3) = 0.250; P(Overcast | No): unsmoothed 0/5 = 0, smoothed (0+1)/(5+3) = 0.125

With $\alpha = 0$ scikit-learn returns the hand result, 0.578. With $\alpha = 1$ the posterior changes slightly, because every likelihood is pulled toward uniform — $2/9$ becomes $3/12$, $3/5$ becomes $4/8$ — and, more importantly, the impossible $P(\text{Overcast} \mid \text{No}) = 0$ becomes $1/8$, so that an overcast day is no longer assigned to Yes with certainty. Smoothing costs a little fidelity to the sample and buys robustness to the values the sample happened not to contain; with 14 days the effect is visible, with 14,000 it would be negligible. scikit-learn's default is $\alpha = 1$.

4.3 Gaussian naive Bayes by hand

The weather example used categorical features, for which a likelihood is a relative frequency. For continuous features a density model is needed, and the Gaussian variant supplies it. Take the six training cases of Unit 1, with the two features mean radius ($x_1$) and mean concave points × 100 ($x_2$), and the same new case $\mathbf{x} = (15, 4)$ that the nearest-centroid classifier called benign:

case $x_1$ radius $x_2$ concave pts × 100 class
1 12 2 benign
2 13 3 benign
3 11 1 benign
4 19 9 malignant
5 21 11 malignant
6 17 7 malignant

Training. The priors are $P(B) = P(M) = 3/6 = 0.5$. The per-class means are those of Unit 1, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_B = (12, 2)$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_M = (19, 9)$. The per-class variances (scikit-learn uses the population variance, dividing by $n_c$, not $n_c - 1$) are, for the benign class, $\sigma^2_{B1} = \tfrac{(12-12)^2 + (13-12)^2 + (11-12)^2}{3} = \tfrac{2}{3}$ and likewise $\sigma^2_{B2} = \tfrac{0 + 1 + 1}{3} = \tfrac{2}{3}$; for the malignant class, $\sigma^2_{M1} = \tfrac{0 + 4 + 4}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3}$ and $\sigma^2_{M2} = \tfrac{0 + 4 + 4}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3}$. The malignant class is four times more dispersed than the benign one in both features.

Classification of $\mathbf{x} = (15, 4)$ uses the log-density of a Gaussian, $\log \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$. For the benign class, $-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi \cdot \tfrac{2}{3}) = -0.716$, so

$\log p(x_1 = 15 \mid B) = -0.716 - \tfrac{9}{4/3} = -0.716 - 6.750 = -7.466$, and $\log p(x_2 = 4 \mid B) = -0.716 - \tfrac{4}{4/3} = -0.716 - 3.000 = -3.716$;

for the malignant class, $-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi \cdot \tfrac{8}{3}) = -1.409$, so

$\log p(x_1 = 15 \mid M) = -1.409 - \tfrac{16}{16/3} = -1.409 - 3.000 = -4.409$, and $\log p(x_2 = 4 \mid M) = -1.409 - \tfrac{25}{16/3} = -1.409 - 4.688 = -6.097$.

Adding the log-prior $\log 0.5 = -0.693$ to each sum: $\log P(B \mid \mathbf{x}) + \text{const} = -0.693 - 7.466 - 3.716 \approx -11.88$ and $\log P(M \mid \mathbf{x}) + \text{const} = -0.693 - 4.409 - 6.097 \approx -11.20$. The malignant class has the larger log-posterior, so naive Bayes classifies the case malignant — the opposite of the nearest-centroid answer of Unit 1, although the case is closer to the benign centroid. Normalising, $P(M \mid \mathbf{x}) = \tfrac{e^{-11.20}}{e^{-11.20} + e^{-11.88}} = \tfrac{1}{1 + e^{-0.676}} \approx 0.663$. The reason is the variance: a point 3 units from the tight benign cluster is more surprising, under a Gaussian model, than a point 4–5 units from the diffuse malignant cluster. The cell below confirms the arithmetic step by step and compares it with scikit-learn.

# Gaussian naive Bayes by hand on the six cases, step by step, then scikit-learn's GaussianNB on the same data.
six = np.array([[12, 2], [13, 3], [11, 1], [19, 9], [21, 11], [17, 7]], dtype=float)
six_y = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0])                      # scikit-learn coding: 1 = benign, 0 = malignant
new = np.array([15.0, 4.0])

def log_gauss(x, mean, var):
    '''Log-density of a univariate normal distribution.'''
    return -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * var) - (x - mean) ** 2 / (2 * var)

log_post = {}
for c, name in [(1, "benign"), (0, "malignant")]:
    Xc = six[six_y == c]
    mean, var = Xc.mean(axis=0), Xc.var(axis=0)           # population variance (ddof=0), as in scikit-learn
    terms = log_gauss(new, mean, var)
    log_post[c] = np.log(len(Xc) / len(six)) + terms.sum()
    print(f"{name:9s}: mean {mean}, var {var.round(3)}, log p(x_j | c) = {terms.round(3)}, log-prior + sum = {log_post[c]:.3f}")
p_M = 1 / (1 + np.exp(log_post[1] - log_post[0]))
print(f"by hand: P(malignant | x) = {p_M:.4f}, P(benign | x) = {1 - p_M:.4f}")
gnb6 = GaussianNB().fit(six, six_y)
print(f"GaussianNB: P(malignant | x) = {gnb6.predict_proba([new])[0, 0]:.4f}  (classes_ = {gnb6.classes_})")

benign   : mean [12.  2.], var [0.667 0.667], log p(x_j | c) = [-7.466 -3.716], log-prior + sum = -11.876
malignant: mean [19.  9.], var [2.667 2.667], log p(x_j | c) = [-4.409 -6.097], log-prior + sum = -11.199
by hand: P(malignant | x) = 0.6629, P(benign | x) = 0.3371
GaussianNB: P(malignant | x) = 0.6629  (classes_ = [0 1])

The hand calculation and scikit-learn agree to four decimals: $P(M \mid \mathbf{x}) \approx 0.663$. (scikit-learn adds a tiny constant to every variance for numerical stability, var_smoothing, a fraction $10^{-9}$ of the largest feature variance; it is invisible at this precision.)

4.4 A naive Bayes classifier in numpy, compared with scikit-learn

The six-case computation generalises without change to $n$ cases and $p$ features. The class below is a complete Gaussian naive Bayes classifier in twenty lines: fit stores the log-priors, means and variances; predict_log_proba sums the per-feature log-densities and normalises with the log-sum-exp trick. It is tested on all 30 features of the breast-cancer data against scikit-learn's implementation; the two should agree to the third decimal on every posterior.

# A Gaussian naive Bayes classifier written with numpy, and a comparison with scikit-learn on all 30 features.
from scipy.special import logsumexp
class HandGaussianNB:
    def fit(self, Xa, ya):
        self.classes_ = np.unique(ya)
        self.log_prior_ = np.log([np.mean(ya == c) for c in self.classes_])
        self.mean_ = np.array([Xa[ya == c].mean(axis=0) for c in self.classes_])
        self.var_ = np.array([Xa[ya == c].var(axis=0) for c in self.classes_])
        self.var_ += 1e-9 * Xa.var(axis=0).max()                          # scikit-learn's var_smoothing, for parity
        return self
    def predict_log_proba(self, Xa):
        ll = np.array([log_gauss(Xa, m, v).sum(axis=1) for m, v in zip(self.mean_, self.var_)]).T   # (n, K)
        joint = ll + self.log_prior_
        return joint - logsumexp(joint, axis=1, keepdims=True)           # normalise over classes in log space
    def predict(self, Xa):
        return self.classes_[np.argmax(self.predict_log_proba(Xa), axis=1)]

X_tr, X_te, _, _ = train_test_split(X.to_numpy(), y.to_numpy(), test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
hand = HandGaussianNB().fit(X_tr, y_tr); skl = GaussianNB().fit(X_tr, y_tr)
diff = np.abs(np.exp(hand.predict_log_proba(X_te)) - skl.predict_proba(X_te)).max()
print(f"largest difference in any posterior between the hand-written and scikit-learn classifiers: {diff:.2e}")
print(f"test accuracy, 30 features: hand-written {np.mean(hand.predict(X_te) == y_te):.3f} | GaussianNB {skl.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
print(f"test accuracy, 2 features : GaussianNB {GaussianNB().fit(X2_tr, y_tr).score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}")

largest difference in any posterior between the hand-written and scikit-learn classifiers: 2.00e-15
test accuracy, 30 features: hand-written 0.924 | GaussianNB 0.924
test accuracy, 2 features : GaussianNB 0.889

The two implementations are numerically identical and reach the same accuracy on the held-out cases: above 0.9 with the 30 features, and slightly lower with the two features of the pictures. Training took one pass over the data to compute 30 means and 30 variances per class — naive Bayes is the fastest classifier to train in this course, which is one reason it remains the baseline for very large problems.

The shape of the boundary follows from the model. For two classes with Gaussian features, the log-posterior ratio is a quadratic function of $\mathbf{x}$ (the squared terms $(x_j - \mu_{cj})^2 / 2\sigma^2_{cj}$ have different coefficients in the two classes when the variances differ), so the boundary where it vanishes is a conic section: an ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. If the variances were equal in both classes the quadratic terms would cancel and the boundary would be a straight line — the same linear form as logistic regression, reached by a different route. The cell below draws the fitted class-conditional Gaussians and the boundary they produce on the two-feature problem.

# The Gaussian model that naive Bayes fits in two dimensions, and the (quadratic) boundary it implies.
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse
gnb2 = GaussianNB().fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.3))
plot_regions(ax, gnb2, X2_te, y_te, "Gaussian naive Bayes: per-class Gaussians (1 and 2 sd) and boundary")
for k, c in enumerate(gnb2.classes_):
    col = ORANGE if c == 0 else BLUE
    for n_sd in (1, 2):   # axis-aligned ellipses: naive Bayes assumes zero within-class correlation
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse(gnb2.theta_[k], 2 * n_sd * np.sqrt(gnb2.var_[k, 0]), 2 * n_sd * np.sqrt(gnb2.var_[k, 1]),
                             fill=False, edgecolor=col, lw=1.2, ls="--" if n_sd == 2 else "-"))
    ax.plot(*gnb2.theta_[k], "X", color=col, ms=10, markeredgecolor="k")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); fig.tight_layout()
print("per-class means (theta_):\n", gnb2.theta_.round(2), "\nper-class variances (var_):\n", gnb2.var_.round(2))

per-class means (theta_):
 [[17.58  8.96]
 [12.04  2.5 ]] 
per-class variances (var_):
 [[10.55 11.54]
 [ 3.18  2.33]]

Figure 5. The model behind the boundary: one axis-aligned Gaussian per class (solid, 1 standard deviation; dashed, 2), with centres marked by crosses, and the resulting decision regions with the test cases drawn on top. The malignant class has much larger variances in both features (printed values), so its Gaussian is wider; the boundary bends around the tight benign cluster and is a curve, not a line. The ellipses are axis-aligned because naive Bayes assumes no correlation between the two features within a class — visibly false for the malignant cases, which trend upward to the right, yet the boundary is still sensible.

4.5 Generative versus discriminative

Naive Bayes and logistic regression (Unit 2) can produce the same family of boundaries, and the comparison between them is instructive. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly and fits its coefficients to make the training labels as probable as possible, with no model of how $\mathbf{x}$ is distributed. Naive Bayes is generative: it models $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$ and $P(y)$ and obtains $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ by Bayes' theorem. Ng and Jordan showed, theoretically and on many datasets, that the two have different learning curves: naive Bayes approaches its asymptotic error with far fewer training cases (its error falls at a rate of order $\log n$ against $n$ for logistic regression), but that asymptote is higher, because its assumptions bias it; logistic regression needs more data and ends up better.[7] With a few dozen cases, prefer naive Bayes; with thousands, prefer the discriminative model. In medical problems, where labelled cases are expensive, the small-sample regime is common, and naive Bayes has a long record in computer-aided diagnosis for exactly that reason.[8]

4.6 Why naive Bayes works although its assumption is false

The puzzle is empirical: naive Bayes classifies well on data in which the features are strongly dependent. Domingos and Pazzani resolved it in 1997.[5] Classification under zero-one loss depends only on which class has the largest posterior, not on the value of the posterior; the independence assumption can distort the posterior probabilities considerably without changing their ranking. They proved that naive Bayes is optimal for some problems in which the assumption is grossly violated — for instance, when the dependencies are distributed evenly across classes and cancel in the comparison — and showed on 28 datasets that its accuracy was not related to the degree of dependence among the features. Hand and Yu added the statistical argument that the simple model has few parameters and therefore low variance: its bias is real, but with small samples the variance of a richer model is worse.[6] The price of the assumption is paid elsewhere: the posteriors are badly calibrated, typically pushed toward 0 and 1 because every correlated feature counts as independent evidence. The two cells below exhibit both halves of the story on the breast-cancer data.

# Half 1: strongly dependent features do not ruin the ranking. Correlations among size features, and NB accuracy
# with 5-fold cross-validation when near-duplicate features are included.
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
size = ["mean radius", "mean perimeter", "mean area"]
print("Correlation among the three size features (within the malignant class):")
print(X.loc[y == 0, size].corr().round(3).to_string())
means10 = [c for c in X.columns if c.startswith("mean ")]
for label, cols in [("3 near-duplicate size features", size), ("10 'mean' features", means10), ("all 30 features", list(X.columns))]:
    acc = cross_val_score(GaussianNB(), X[cols], y, cv=cv5)
    print(f"NB accuracy with {label:32s}: {acc.mean():.3f} ± {acc.std():.3f}")

# Half 2: the posteriors are over-confident. Fraction of test cases given an extreme posterior, NB vs logistic regression.
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
lr30 = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
for name, model in [("Gaussian naive Bayes", skl), ("logistic regression", lr30)]:
    p = model.predict_proba(X_te).max(axis=1)
    print(f"{name:20s}: accuracy {model.score(X_te, y_te):.3f} | {np.mean(p > 0.99):.1%} of test cases get a posterior > 0.99 | "
          f"mean posterior of the chosen class {p.mean():.3f}")

Correlation among the three size features (within the malignant class):
                mean radius  mean perimeter  mean area
mean radius           1.000           0.995      0.990
mean perimeter        0.995           1.000      0.987
mean area             0.990           0.987      1.000
NB accuracy with 3 near-duplicate size features  : 0.886 ± 0.021
NB accuracy with 10 'mean' features              : 0.910 ± 0.016
NB accuracy with all 30 features                 : 0.939 ± 0.020
Gaussian naive Bayes: accuracy 0.924 | 95.3% of test cases get a posterior > 0.99 | mean posterior of the chosen class 0.993
logistic regression : accuracy 0.959 | 71.9% of test cases get a posterior > 0.99 | mean posterior of the chosen class 0.961

The first cell shows the two halves of the Domingos–Pazzani argument. Radius, perimeter and area are correlated above 0.98 within a class; treating them as independent is a gross violation of the assumption, yet adding the 20 further features — many of them equally redundant — does not harm the cross-validated accuracy. The second cell shows the price: naive Bayes assigns a posterior above 0.99 to about 95 % of the test cases, considerably more often than logistic regression does at a higher accuracy, because each redundant feature is counted as fresh evidence. When the output of a classifier is to be used as a probability — to set a cost-sensitive threshold as in Section 3.2, or to be shown to a clinician — naive Bayes posteriors should be re-calibrated on held-out data (Supplement S1 discusses calibration), or a discriminative model should be preferred.

Common misconception

"Naive Bayes is accurate, so its probabilities can be trusted." Accuracy depends on the ranking of the posteriors; calibration depends on their values. Naive Bayes often has the first without the second. A 0.99 from a naive Bayes model on correlated features is not a 99 % chance of malignancy; it is a vote in which the same witness was counted several times.

4.7 Naive Bayes for counts and binary features

The Gaussian variant suits continuous measurements. For count data — words in a clinical note, reads mapped to a gene, pixels in a grey-level image — the multinomial variant models each class by a vector of category probabilities estimated as smoothed frequencies, and the Bernoulli variant models the presence or absence of each feature. The cell below applies both to the 1,797 handwritten digits of Unit 1, treating each 8 × 8 image as 64 counts (multinomial) or as 64 binary "ink present" features (Bernoulli), and also fits the Gaussian variant for comparison. The point is not the accuracy — the digits are a stand-in for any bag-of-features representation — but that the same algorithm serves three data types by changing only the one-dimensional model.

# Multinomial and Bernoulli naive Bayes on the digits, treated as counts and as binary features; Gaussian for comparison.
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB
digits = datasets.load_digits()
Xd, yd = digits.data, digits.target
for name, model, Xin in [("MultinomialNB (pixel intensities as counts)", MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0), Xd),
                         ("BernoulliNB (pixel > 7 as 'ink present')", BernoulliNB(alpha=1.0), (Xd > 7).astype(int)),
                         ("GaussianNB (intensities as continuous)", GaussianNB(), Xd)]:
    acc = cross_val_score(model, Xin, yd, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
    print(f"{name:45s}: 5-fold accuracy {acc.mean():.3f} ± {acc.std():.3f}")

MultinomialNB (pixel intensities as counts)  : 5-fold accuracy 0.901 ± 0.011
BernoulliNB (pixel > 7 as 'ink present')     : 5-fold accuracy 0.888 ± 0.013
GaussianNB (intensities as continuous)       : 5-fold accuracy 0.851 ± 0.025

The multinomial and Bernoulli variants reach a comparable accuracy on ten classes with a single pass over the data; the Gaussian variant does worse here because pixel intensities are bounded, skewed and often exactly zero, which a normal distribution describes poorly. Choosing the variant whose one-dimensional model matches the feature type is the only modelling decision naive Bayes asks of the analyst.

In the cell of Section 4.4, replace the test split with a very small training sample — keep only the first 20 training cases (X_tr[:20], y_tr[:20]) — and compare the test accuracy of GaussianNB and of the logistic-regression pipeline of Section 4.6 trained on the same 20 cases. 5. Bayesian networks

5.1 From the joint distribution to a graph

Naive Bayes makes one extreme assumption — all features independent given the class — to make a joint distribution tractable. A Bayesian network (belief network, probabilistic graphical model) makes the assumptions explicit and selective: it is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose nodes are random variables and whose arrows encode direct dependence, together with, for each node, a conditional probability table (CPT) giving the distribution of the node for each combination of values of its parents. The semantics of the graph is a single equation, the factorisation of the joint distribution:

$$P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_m) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} P\big(X_i \mid \mathrm{parents}(X_i)\big)$$ Each variable depends directly only on its parents in the graph. The equation follows from the chain rule of probability, $P(X_1, \dots, X_m) = \prod_i P(X_i \mid X_1, \dots, X_{i-1})$, once each variable is assumed independent of its non-descendants given its parents (the local Markov property).

The formalism was developed by Judea Pearl in the 1980s as a representation of uncertain knowledge for expert systems, replacing the ad-hoc certainty factors of MYCIN (Unit 1) with coherent probability,[9],[10] and the first efficient general inference algorithm was published by Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter in 1988 with a medical example that has become the standard teaching network: a fictitious chest clinic in which a visit to Asia, smoking, tuberculosis, lung cancer and bronchitis explain a chest X-ray and dyspnoea.[11] This section uses a reduced version of that network with five binary variables — Smoking (S), lung Cancer (C), Bronchitis (B), positive chest X-ray (X) and Dyspnoea (D) — keeping the published conditional probabilities for the retained arrows. The figure below draws it.

Figure 6. The network. Smoking is a risk factor for both lung cancer and bronchitis; lung cancer produces an abnormal chest X-ray and dyspnoea; bronchitis produces dyspnoea but not an abnormal X-ray. There is no arrow from Smoking to X-ray: the graph asserts that, once the presence or absence of cancer is known, smoking history carries no further information about the X-ray. Every such missing arrow is an assumption of conditional independence.

The factorisation implied by Figure 6 is

$$P(S, C, B, X, D) = P(S)\; P(C \mid S)\; P(B \mid S)\; P(X \mid C)\; P(D \mid C, B).$$

Counting parameters shows what the graph buys. The full joint distribution of five binary variables has $2^5 - 1 = 31$ free probabilities. The factorised form needs one number for $P(S)$, two each for $P(C \mid S)$, $P(B \mid S)$ and $P(X \mid C)$, and four for $P(D \mid C, B)$: eleven in total, each of which is a quantity a clinician can state or a registry can estimate ("the probability of lung cancer in a smoker"). The five tables are the CPTs; the cell below enters them as pandas DataFrames, with the values of the original network.[11]

# Conditional probability tables (CPTs) of the reduced Asia network. Each table gives P(variable = yes | parents).
cpt = {
    "S": pd.DataFrame({"P(S=yes)": [0.50]}, index=["(no parents)"]),
    "C": pd.DataFrame({"P(C=yes | S)": [0.01, 0.10]}, index=pd.Index(["S=no", "S=yes"])),
    "B": pd.DataFrame({"P(B=yes | S)": [0.30, 0.60]}, index=pd.Index(["S=no", "S=yes"])),
    "X": pd.DataFrame({"P(X=yes | C)": [0.05, 0.98]}, index=pd.Index(["C=no", "C=yes"])),
    "D": pd.DataFrame({"P(D=yes | C, B)": [0.10, 0.80, 0.70, 0.90]},
                      index=pd.Index(["C=no, B=no", "C=no, B=yes", "C=yes, B=no", "C=yes, B=yes"])),
}
for k, t in cpt.items():
    print(f"CPT of {names[k].replace(chr(10), ' ')}:"); print(t.to_string(), "\n")
n_params = sum(len(t) for t in cpt.values())
print(f"free parameters in the factorised model: {n_params}  (versus 2^5 - 1 = {2**5 - 1} for the unrestricted joint)")

5.2 Inference by enumeration

Inference in a Bayesian network means computing the posterior distribution of some variables (the query) given observed values of others (the evidence), with the remaining variables unobserved. The simplest exact algorithm is enumeration: write out the joint probability of every complete assignment using the factorisation, keep the rows consistent with the evidence, and sum over the unobserved variables:

$$P(C \mid D = \text{yes}, X = \text{yes}) = \frac{\sum_{S, B} P(S, C, B, X = \text{yes}, D = \text{yes})}{\sum_{S, C, B} P(S, C, B, X = \text{yes}, D = \text{yes})}.$$

The numerator is the joint probability of the query and the evidence, the denominator is the marginal probability of the evidence, and their ratio is Bayes' theorem in disguise: this is exactly the computation of Section 2.2, with the network supplying the likelihood and the prior. For five binary variables the joint has 32 rows and enumeration is instant; its cost grows as $2^m$ and becomes impractical beyond a few dozen variables, which is why the algorithm of Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter, which exploits the graph to sum locally, mattered.[11] The cell below builds the 32-row joint table and a general query function.

# The full joint distribution of the network (32 rows), built from the CPTs, and a query function by enumeration.
import itertools
pS = 0.50; pC = {0: 0.01, 1: 0.10}; pB = {0: 0.30, 1: 0.60}; pX = {0: 0.05, 1: 0.98}
pD = {(0, 0): 0.10, (0, 1): 0.80, (1, 0): 0.70, (1, 1): 0.90}                # keyed by (C, B)
def bern(p, value):
    '''Probability that a binary variable with P(yes) = p takes the given value (1 = yes, 0 = no).'''
    return p if value == 1 else 1 - p
rows = []
for s, c, b, x, d in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=5):
    p = bern(pS, s) * bern(pC[s], c) * bern(pB[s], b) * bern(pX[c], x) * bern(pD[(c, b)], d)
    rows.append(dict(S=s, C=c, B=b, X=x, D=d, p=p))
joint = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"rows: {len(joint)} | probabilities sum to {joint.p.sum():.6f}")

def query(target, **evidence):
    '''P(target = yes | evidence) by enumeration: sum the consistent rows, then normalise.'''
    sub = joint
    for var, val in evidence.items():
        sub = sub[sub[var] == val]
    return sub.loc[sub[target] == 1, "p"].sum() / sub["p"].sum()

print(f"P(C = yes)                      = {query('C'):.4f}   (prior probability of lung cancer)")
print(f"P(C = yes | D = yes)            = {query('C', D=1):.4f}")
print(f"P(C = yes | D = yes, X = yes)   = {query('C', D=1, X=1):.4f}")
joint.sort_values("p", ascending=False).head(4).round(4)

rows: 32 | probabilities sum to 1.000000
P(C = yes)                      = 0.0550   (prior probability of lung cancer)
P(C = yes | D = yes)            = 0.1036
P(C = yes | D = yes, X = yes)   = 0.6938
S C B X D p
0 0 0 0 0 0 0.2963

The prior probability of lung cancer in this population is 0.055. Dyspnoea raises it to about 0.10 — a modest increase, because bronchitis explains dyspnoea equally well — and a positive X-ray in addition raises it to about 0.69, because the X-ray is specific to cancer in this network. The most probable complete states (table) are, unsurprisingly, the healthy ones. The next cell adds pieces of evidence one at a time in a clinically natural order and watches the posterior of cancer move, including the effect of learning that the patient does not smoke, and of learning that bronchitis is present.

# How the posterior of lung cancer moves as evidence accumulates (and as alternative explanations appear).
scenarios = [("no evidence", {}), ("dyspnoea", dict(D=1)), ("dyspnoea + positive X-ray", dict(D=1, X=1)),
             ("dyspnoea + X-ray + smoker", dict(D=1, X=1, S=1)), ("dyspnoea + X-ray + non-smoker", dict(D=1, X=1, S=0)),
             ("dyspnoea + bronchitis known", dict(D=1, B=1)), ("positive X-ray only", dict(X=1)),
             ("negative X-ray + dyspnoea", dict(X=0, D=1))]
post = pd.DataFrame({"evidence": [s for s, _ in scenarios], "P(cancer | evidence)": [query("C", **e) for _, e in scenarios]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))
ax.barh(post["evidence"], post["P(cancer | evidence)"], color=[ORANGE if v > 0.3 else BLUE for v in post.iloc[:, 1]])
for i, v in enumerate(post.iloc[:, 1]):
    ax.text(v + 0.01, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_xlabel("P(lung cancer = yes | evidence)")
ax.set_title("Posterior probability of lung cancer under different evidence"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 7. Posterior probability of lung cancer under eight evidence sets. Each piece of evidence moves the posterior through the arrows of the graph: dyspnoea and the X-ray are effects of cancer and raise it; smoking is a cause and raises it further; non-smoking lowers it. Two rows deserve attention. Knowing that bronchitis is present lowers the posterior of cancer given dyspnoea (compare the "dyspnoea" and "dyspnoea + bronchitis known" bars): bronchitis explains away the dyspnoea, so less of it remains to be explained by cancer, even though cancer and bronchitis are not directly connected. And a negative X-ray with dyspnoea leaves cancer very unlikely, because the X-ray has a sensitivity of 0.98 for cancer in this network.

5.3 d-separation: reading independence off the graph

Which variables are independent of which, given what, can be read from the graph without any arithmetic, by a criterion Pearl called d-separation.[10] Three local structures account for everything:

  • Chain $S \rightarrow C \rightarrow X$: smoking influences the X-ray only through cancer. $S$ and $X$ are dependent, but become independent once $C$ is observed — the chain is blocked by conditioning on the middle node.
  • Fork (common cause) $C \leftarrow S \rightarrow B$: cancer and bronchitis are associated in the population because both are caused by smoking, and become independent once smoking is known. Conditioning on the common cause blocks the fork.
  • Collider (common effect) $C \rightarrow D \leftarrow B$: cancer and bronchitis are independent (given smoking) until the common effect, dyspnoea, is observed; conditioning on a collider opens the path and makes the two causes dependent — this is the mechanism of explaining away seen in Figure 7.

Two variables are d-separated, and hence conditionally independent, when every path between them is blocked. The cell below verifies the three statements numerically by enumeration.

# Numerical check of the three d-separation statements.
chain = (query("X", C=1), query("X", C=1, S=1), query("X", C=1, S=0))
print(f"Chain  S -> C -> X   : P(X | C=yes) = {chain[0]:.3f}, P(X | C=yes, S=yes) = {chain[1]:.3f}, "
      f"P(X | C=yes, S=no) = {chain[2]:.3f}   (equal: the chain is blocked by C)")
fork = (query("B"), query("B", C=1), query("B", S=1), query("B", S=1, C=1))
print(f"Fork   C <- S -> B   : P(B) = {fork[0]:.3f} vs P(B | C=yes) = {fork[1]:.3f} (dependent); "
      f"given S=yes: P(B | S) = {fork[2]:.3f} vs P(B | S, C=yes) = {fork[3]:.3f} (independent)")
coll = (query("C", S=1), query("C", S=1, B=1), query("C", S=1, D=1), query("C", S=1, D=1, B=1))
print(f"Collider C -> D <- B : given S=yes, P(C | S) = {coll[0]:.3f} vs P(C | S, B=yes) = {coll[1]:.3f} (independent); "
      f"given S=yes and D=yes: P(C | S, D) = {coll[2]:.3f} vs P(C | S, D, B=yes) = {coll[3]:.3f} (dependent: explaining away)")

Chain  S -> C -> X   : P(X | C=yes) = 0.980, P(X | C=yes, S=yes) = 0.980, P(X | C=yes, S=no) = 0.980   (equal: the chain is blocked by C)
Fork   C <- S -> B   : P(B) = 0.450 vs P(B | C=yes) = 0.573 (dependent); given S=yes: P(B | S) = 0.600 vs P(B | S, C=yes) = 0.600 (independent)
Collider C -> D <- B : given S=yes, P(C | S) = 0.100 vs P(C | S, B=yes) = 0.100 (independent); given S=yes and D=yes: P(C | S, D) = 0.149 vs P(C | S, D, B=yes) = 0.111 (dependent: explaining away)

The numbers confirm the graph. The X-ray probability given cancer is the same whether or not the patient smokes (chain blocked); bronchitis is associated with cancer marginally but not once smoking is fixed (fork blocked); and cancer and bronchitis are independent given smoking until dyspnoea is observed, whereupon knowing bronchitis lowers the probability of cancer (collider opened). The practical importance of the third case is large: selecting patients on a common effect — admission to hospital, a positive screening result — induces associations between its causes that do not exist in the population, a bias that epidemiology calls collider or Berkson's bias.

5.4 Naive Bayes as a Bayesian network, and learning networks from data

Naive Bayes is the Bayesian network in which the class is the single parent of every feature and there are no other arrows: $P(y, x_1, \dots, x_p) = P(y) \prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$, exactly the factorisation of Section 4.1. Seen this way, its assumption is a very sparse graph, and the natural remedy for a violated assumption is to add arrows. Friedman, Geiger and Goldszmidt did precisely that: their tree-augmented naive Bayes (TAN) lets each feature have one additional parent among the other features, chosen to capture the strongest within-class dependence, and improves on naive Bayes on most of the benchmark datasets they tested while remaining cheap to learn.[14]

Both the parameters and the structure of a Bayesian network can be learned from data. Parameter learning with a known graph and complete data is counting: the maximum-likelihood estimate of $P(X_i = x \mid \mathrm{parents} = u)$ is the fraction of cases with parents $= u$ in which $X_i = x$, usually smoothed with a Dirichlet prior so that unseen combinations do not receive probability zero; Heckerman's tutorial is the standard reference for both this and the Bayesian treatment of missing data.[13] Structure learning searches the space of DAGs for one that scores well (by penalised likelihood or marginal likelihood) or that is consistent with the conditional independences found in the data; the search is combinatorial and in practice is guided by expert constraints such as a causal ordering of the variables. In biomedicine, networks have been built from expert knowledge, from data, or from both, for diagnosis, prognosis and treatment selection; Lucas and colleagues review the field and its difficulties, chief among them the elicitation of probabilities from clinicians and the validation of a model that is more than a classifier.[15] Early medical systems built on this technology — the MUNIN network for electromyographic diagnosis, the Pathfinder system for lymph-node pathology — are among the examples that review discusses. The cell below shows parameter learning in its simplest form: it draws a synthetic registry of patients from the network by forward sampling (each variable sampled after its parents) and recovers the CPTs by counting.

# Parameter learning = counting. Sample 5,000 synthetic patients from the network, then re-estimate two CPTs from the sample.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
S = rng.random(n) < pS
C = rng.random(n) < np.where(S, pC[1], pC[0])
B = rng.random(n) < np.where(S, pB[1], pB[0])
Xr = rng.random(n) < np.where(C, pX[1], pX[0])
D = rng.random(n) < np.array([pD[(int(c), int(b))] for c, b in zip(C, B)])
registry = pd.DataFrame({"S": S, "C": C, "B": B, "X": Xr, "D": D}).astype(int)

est_C = registry.groupby("S")["C"].mean().rename("estimated P(C=yes | S)").to_frame()
est_C["true"] = [pC[0], pC[1]]; est_C["n cases"] = registry.groupby("S").size()
est_D = registry.groupby(["C", "B"])["D"].mean().rename("estimated P(D=yes | C, B)").to_frame()
est_D["true"] = [pD[k] for k in est_D.index]; est_D["n cases"] = registry.groupby(["C", "B"]).size()
print(est_C.round(3).to_string(), "\n"); print(est_D.round(3).to_string())

   estimated P(C=yes | S)  true  n cases
S                                       
0                   0.007  0.01     2493
1                   0.097  0.10     2507 

     estimated P(D=yes | C, B)  true  n cases
C B                                          
0 0                      0.105   0.1     2700
  1                      0.800   0.8     2041
1 0                      0.704   0.7      108
  1                      0.861   0.9      151

The estimates track the true values, and their precision depends on the number of cases in each parent configuration: $P(D \mid C = \text{yes}, B = \text{yes})$ is estimated from only about 150 patients who have both conditions, and is correspondingly less precise than the entries estimated from thousands. This is the general lesson of parameter learning: the data requirement grows with the number of parent configurations, so a node with many parents needs a large registry or a prior.

Bridge to Unit 1 and to bioinformatics

A Bayesian network is the modern form of the "reasoning with uncertainty" that Unit 1 attributed to symbolic AI: the graph is knowledge, written by hand or learned, and inference is deduction with probabilities. The same formalism underlies the hidden Markov models used for gene finding and profile alignment in BGM324 — an HMM is a Bayesian network unrolled over the positions of a sequence — and the pedigree analyses of genetic linkage, where the DAG is the family tree.

Add the missing node of the original Asia network: a visit to Asia (A, prior 0.01) raises the probability of tuberculosis (T: 0.05 if A, 0.01 otherwise), and either tuberculosis or cancer produces the positive X-ray and the dyspnoea (replace C by "T or C" in those two CPTs). 6. k-Nearest Neighbours

6.1 The rule, by hand

The k-nearest-neighbours (k-NN) rule is the simplest memory-based classifier, and the archetype of what the literature calls a lazy learner: it builds no explicit model at training time — training consists of storing the labelled sample — and defers all computation to the moment a prediction is requested. To classify a new case $\mathbf{x}$: compute its distance to every stored case, select the $k$ closest, and assign the majority class among them; for regression, predict the mean of their targets. The rule was proposed in a 1951 technical report by Fix and Hodges for the US Air Force, which remained unpublished until 1989,[16] and its key theoretical property was established by Cover and Hart in 1967: as the training sample grows without bound, the error of the 1-nearest-neighbour rule is at most twice the Bayes error, for any distribution of the data.[17] In other words, half of the information needed for optimal classification is contained in the single nearest neighbour — a remarkable statement for a rule with no model, no training and one free parameter.

Worked example. With the six training cases of Section 4.3 and the new case $\mathbf{x} = (15, 4)$, the Euclidean distances are:

case features class $d^2 = (15 - x_1)^2 + (4 - x_2)^2$ $d$
1 (12, 2) benign $9 + 4 = 13$ 3.61
2 (13, 3) benign $4 + 1 = 5$ 2.24
3 (11, 1) benign $16 + 9 = 25$ 5.00
4 (19, 9) malignant $16 + 25 = 41$ 6.40
5 (21, 11) malignant $36 + 49 = 85$ 9.22
6 (17, 7) malignant $4 + 9 = 13$ 3.61

For $k = 1$ the nearest case is case 2 (benign), so the prediction is benign. For $k = 3$ the three nearest are case 2 ($d = 2.24$) and then cases 1 and 6, which are tied at $d = 3.61$; whichever tie-break is used, the three neighbours include two benign cases, and the majority prediction is again benign. The distance-weighted variant of Section 6.6, in which each neighbour votes with weight $1/d$, gives benign $1/2.24 + 1/3.61 = 0.446 + 0.277 = 0.723$ against malignant $0.277$ — benign by a wider margin. Note that the three classifiers of this unit now disagree about this one point: nearest centroid and k-NN say benign, Gaussian naive Bayes says malignant, and the point lies in the overlap where no method can be sure. The cell confirms the table.

# k-NN by hand on the six cases: distances, the k nearest, and the majority vote, confirmed with scikit-learn.
d = np.sqrt(((six - new) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
table = pd.DataFrame({"x1": six[:, 0], "x2": six[:, 1], "class": np.where(six_y == 1, "benign", "malignant"),
                      "distance": d.round(3)}, index=pd.RangeIndex(1, 7, name="case")).sort_values("distance")
print(table.to_string())
for k in (1, 3):
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(six, six_y)
    dist, idx = knn.kneighbors([new])
    votes = np.bincount(six_y[idx[0]], minlength=2)
    print(f"k={k}: neighbours = cases {idx[0] + 1}, votes (malignant, benign) = {votes}, prediction = "
          f"{'benign' if knn.predict([new])[0] == 1 else 'malignant'}")
wknn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3, weights="distance").fit(six, six_y)
print(f"k=3, weights=1/d: P(benign) = {wknn.predict_proba([new])[0, 1]:.3f}")

        x1    x2      class  distance
case                                 
2     13.0   3.0     benign     2.236

6     17.0   7.0  malignant     3.606
