scikit-learn reproduces the table and the votes. Observe the tie at $d = 3.61$: kneighbors lists case 6 before case 1, an arbitrary by-product of the search algorithm rather than a principled choice. Here it is harmless, because with $k = 3$ both tied cases are among the neighbours; with $k = 2$ the tie would decide which case enters the vote. Ties in the vote itself (possible when $k$ is even) are broken in favour of the class that appears first in classes_; using an odd $k$ for binary problems avoids them.

The vote depends on $k$, and the dependence can flip the answer. The lecture slides illustrate this with a configuration that the cell below reproduces: a new point whose three nearest neighbours are two triangles and one square, and whose five nearest neighbours are two triangles and three squares. With $k = 3$ the point is a triangle; with $k = 5$ it is a square. Nothing about the data changed — only the size of the neighbourhood consulted.

# The classic toy example: the same new point is a 'triangle' with k = 3 and a 'square' with k = 5.
toy_X = np.array([[0.6, 0.8], [-0.7, 0.7],                      # two triangles close to the new point
                  [1.0, -0.5],                                  # one square slightly farther
                  [-1.2, -1.0], [1.3, 1.1],                     # two more squares, farther still
                  [-2.4, 1.8], [2.6, -1.9], [-2.0, -2.5], [2.8, 2.4], [0.3, 3.0]])   # the rest, farther away
toy_y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0])               # 0 = triangle, 1 = square
query_pt = np.array([[0.0, 0.0]])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 3.9), sharey=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes, (3, 5)):
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(toy_X, toy_y)
    dist, idx = knn.kneighbors(query_pt)
    votes = np.bincount(toy_y[idx[0]], minlength=2); pred = "triangle" if knn.predict(query_pt)[0] == 0 else "square"
    print(f"k = {k}: neighbours {idx[0]}, votes triangles {votes[0]} / squares {votes[1]}  ->  {pred}")
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), dist[0, -1] * 1.02, fill=False, ls="--", color=GREY))
    ax.scatter(*toy_X[toy_y == 0].T, marker="^", s=90, color=BLUE, label="triangle class")
    ax.scatter(*toy_X[toy_y == 1].T, marker="s", s=70, color=ORANGE, label="square class")
    ax.scatter(0, 0, marker="*", s=260, color=GREEN, edgecolor="k", zorder=5, label="new point")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-3.2, 3.4); ax.set_ylim(-3.2, 3.4)
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}: {votes[0]} triangles, {votes[1]} square{'s' if votes[1] != 1 else ''}  →  {pred}")
fig.legend(*axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02))
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))

k = 3: neighbours [1 0 2], votes triangles 2 / squares 1  ->  triangle
k = 5: neighbours [1 0 2 3 4], votes triangles 2 / squares 3  ->  square

Figure 8. The same ten stored cases and the same new point (star), with the neighbourhood of the $k$ nearest cases drawn as a dashed circle. With $k = 3$ the circle contains two triangles and one square and the point is classified as a triangle; with $k = 5$ it contains two triangles and three squares and the point becomes a square. The flip is not a defect of the rule but a reminder that $k$ is a modelling choice: Section 6.4 shows how to make it by validation rather than by inspection.

6.2 What "nearest" means: distance metrics

The rule depends entirely on the definition of distance. For two feature vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$, the Minkowski distance of order $q$ is

$$d_q(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \Big( \sum_{j=1}^{p} |a_j - b_j|^q \Big)^{1/q},$$

of which the Euclidean distance ($q = 2$, the straight-line distance) and the Manhattan or city-block distance ($q = 1$, the sum of absolute differences along each axis) are the common cases; as $q \to \infty$ the distance tends to the largest single coordinate difference (Chebyshev). Euclidean distance is the default and is appropriate for continuous features measured on consistent scales; Manhattan distance is less dominated by a single large deviation and is often preferred when the features are not normally distributed or the dimension is high;[21] the general Minkowski distance, with its tunable order $q$ (the parameter p of scikit-learn), interpolates between them and is itself a hyper-parameter that can be chosen by validation. For binary or categorical features the Hamming distance (number of mismatching positions) is the analogue, and for text or expression profiles the cosine or correlation distance, which ignores overall magnitude. The cell below computes the three Minkowski distances between two real cases and draws the set of points at unit distance from the origin under each, which is the shape a neighbourhood takes.

# Three Minkowski distances between the same two cases, and the unit 'circle' of each metric.
from scipy.spatial.distance import minkowski
a, b = X2_tr[0], X2_tr[1]
print(f"case A = {a.round(2)}, case B = {b.round(2)}")
for q, nm in [(1, "Manhattan"), (2, "Euclidean"), (3, "Minkowski q=3"), (np.inf, "Chebyshev")]:
    print(f"  {nm:14s} distance = {minkowski(a, b, p=q):.3f}")
th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400); u = np.c_[np.cos(th), np.sin(th)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 4))
for q, nm, col in [(1, "Manhattan (q = 1)", ORANGE), (2, "Euclidean (q = 2)", BLUE), (np.inf, "Chebyshev (q → ∞)", GREEN)]:
    r = 1 / np.linalg.norm(u, ord=q, axis=1)                    # scale each direction to unit q-norm
    ax.plot(u[:, 0] * r, u[:, 1] * r, color=col, label=nm)
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$a_1 - b_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$a_2 - b_2$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Points at distance 1 from the origin"); fig.tight_layout()

case A = [13.2  1.1], case B = [11.22  0.64]
  Manhattan      distance = 2.442
  Euclidean      distance = 2.033
  Minkowski q=3  distance = 1.988
  Chebyshev      distance = 1.980

Figure 9. The set of points at unit distance from the centre under three metrics: a diamond for Manhattan, a circle for Euclidean, a square for Chebyshev. A k-NN neighbourhood has the shape of the metric's unit ball, so the choice of metric decides which cases count as neighbours. The printed distances between two real cases rank in the expected order: Manhattan ≥ Euclidean ≥ Chebyshev, since $d_1 \geq d_2 \geq d_\infty$ always.

6.3 Feature scaling is not optional

Every Minkowski distance adds squared (or absolute) differences across features as if they were commensurable. They are not: in the breast-cancer data, "mean area" ranges over hundreds of square micrometres while "mean fractal dimension" varies in the second decimal place, so the Euclidean distance between two patients is, numerically, the difference in area and almost nothing else. A k-NN classifier on the raw features is a one-feature classifier that does not know it. The remedy is to standardise every feature to zero mean and unit variance (or to scale it to [0, 1]) using statistics computed on the training data only, so that each feature contributes on an equal footing. The cell below measures the damage done by omitting this step.

# The failure without scaling: feature ranges, the share of the total variance owned by two features, and k-NN accuracy.
rng_ = X.describe().loc[["min", "max"]].T
print("Smallest and largest feature ranges:")
print(pd.concat([rng_.sort_values("max").head(2), rng_.sort_values("max").tail(2)]).round(3).to_string())
var_share = X.var() / X.var().sum()
print(f"\nShare of the total feature variance held by 'worst area' + 'mean area': {var_share[['worst area', 'mean area']].sum():.1%}")
raw = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5), X, y, cv=cv5)
scaled = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)), X, y, cv=cv5)
area_only = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5), X[["worst area", "mean area"]], y, cv=cv5)
print(f"\n5-NN, 5-fold CV accuracy: raw 30 features {raw.mean():.3f} ± {raw.std():.3f} | "
      f"only the two area features {area_only.mean():.3f} | standardised 30 features {scaled.mean():.3f} ± {scaled.std():.3f}")

Smallest and largest feature ranges:
                             min       max
fractal dimension error    0.001     0.030
smoothness error           0.002     0.031
mean area                143.500  2501.000
worst area               185.200  4254.000

Share of the total feature variance held by 'worst area' + 'mean area': 99.1%

5-NN, 5-fold CV accuracy: raw 30 features 0.932 ± 0.019 | only the two area features 0.932 | standardised 30 features 0.965 ± 0.021

Two features own almost all of the variance, and k-NN on the raw 30 features performs about as well as k-NN on those two features alone — the other 28 are numerically invisible. Standardising them raises the cross-validated accuracy by about three percentage points, which on this easy problem is roughly half of the remaining errors. The same applies to the support vector machine of Section 7 and to every method based on distances or inner products; naive Bayes and decision trees (Unit 4) are the exceptions, since they treat each feature on its own scale. In scikit-learn the scaler and the classifier are combined into a Pipeline precisely so that the scaler is fitted inside each cross-validation fold and never sees the test cases.

Common misconception

"Standardising the whole dataset before splitting is harmless." The mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset include the test cases, so the test cases have leaked into the training procedure. The leak is small for scaling and large for other preprocessing steps (feature selection, imputation), and the habit of putting every step inside a pipeline avoids it uniformly. Supplement S1 treats leakage in detail.

6.4 Choosing k

The parameter $k$ controls the smoothness of the rule. With $k = 1$ every training case is classified correctly — its nearest neighbour is itself — and the boundary wraps around every isolated case, including mislabelled or atypical ones: the rule has memorised the sample, which is overfitting in its purest form. As $k$ grows the vote averages over a larger neighbourhood, the boundary smooths, and the influence of any single case fades; in the limit $k = n$ every point is assigned the majority class of the whole sample. The right $k$ balances these effects and is chosen by validation, never by the training error. The cell below computes a validation curve: training accuracy and 5-fold cross-validated accuracy against $k$, on the standardised 30 features.

# Validation curve for k: training accuracy versus cross-validated accuracy (standardised 30 features).
from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve
ks = np.arange(1, 61)
tr_acc, cv_acc = validation_curve(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()), X, y,
                                  param_name="kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors", param_range=ks, cv=cv5)
best_k = ks[np.argmax(cv_acc.mean(axis=1))]
print(f"k = 1: training accuracy {tr_acc.mean(1)[0]:.3f}, CV accuracy {cv_acc.mean(1)[0]:.3f}")
print(f"best k by CV: {best_k} (CV accuracy {cv_acc.mean(1).max():.3f}); CV accuracy at k = 60: {cv_acc.mean(1)[-1]:.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.5))
ax.plot(ks, tr_acc.mean(1), "o-", ms=3, color=GREY, label="training accuracy")
ax.plot(ks, cv_acc.mean(1), "o-", ms=3, color=BLUE, label="5-fold CV accuracy")
ax.fill_between(ks, cv_acc.mean(1) - cv_acc.std(1), cv_acc.mean(1) + cv_acc.std(1), color="#dfe7f1")
ax.axvline(best_k, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=1, label=f"best k = {best_k}")
ax.set_xlabel("k (number of neighbours)"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_ylim(0.9, 1.005)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax.set_title("Validation curve of k-NN on the breast-cancer data"); fig.tight_layout()

k = 1: training accuracy 1.000, CV accuracy 0.958
best k by CV: 12 (CV accuracy 0.968); CV accuracy at k = 60: 0.949

Figure 10. Training accuracy (grey) and cross-validated accuracy (blue, with ± 1 standard deviation across folds) as $k$ runs from 1 to 60. At $k = 1$ the training accuracy is 1.000 by construction while the cross-validated accuracy is lower; the gap is the overfitting. The cross-validated curve rises to a broad maximum around $k \approx 10$ and then declines slowly as the neighbourhood becomes too large to follow the boundary. The maximum is broad and the fold-to-fold band is wide: any $k$ between about 5 and 20 is defensible, and the single "best" value should not be over-interpreted (Supplement S1 discusses the one-standard-error rule).

The effect of $k$ on the shape of the boundary is best seen in two dimensions. The next cell fits k-NN with $k = 1$, $5$ and $25$ to the two-feature problem (standardised inside a pipeline so that the two features contribute equally) and draws the regions.

# Decision regions of k-NN for k = 1, 5 and 25 on the two-feature problem.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.3), sharey=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes, (1, 5, 25)):
    knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)).fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
    plot_regions(ax, knn, X2_tr, y_tr, f"k = {k}: train {knn.score(X2_tr, y_tr):.3f}, test {knn.score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}")
    if ax is not axes[0]: ax.set_ylabel("")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 11. Decision regions for $k = 1$, $5$ and $25$, with the training cases drawn. With $k = 1$ the boundary is a jagged frontier with islands around every isolated case: every training case is on the correct side (training accuracy 1.000), and the islands are noise. With $k = 5$ most islands disappear; with $k = 25$ the boundary is smooth and the few remaining training errors are the cases deep inside the other class's territory, which no reasonable rule should accommodate. The test accuracies, printed in the titles, are close for $k = 5$ and $25$ and lower for $k = 1$.

6.5 The curse of dimensionality

The k-NN rule assumes that near neighbours exist. In high-dimensional spaces they may not, in a precise sense that Richard Bellman named the curse of dimensionality in 1961[20] and that Beyer and colleagues made specific for nearest-neighbour search in 1999: as the number of dimensions $p$ grows, under broad conditions, the distance from a query point to its nearest neighbour approaches the distance to its farthest neighbour, so that the contrast between "near" and "far" vanishes and the nearest neighbour is no longer meaningful.[21] The intuition is that in $p$ dimensions a neighbourhood that captures a fixed fraction of the data must extend, along each axis, over a fraction of the range that approaches 1 as $p$ grows: to enclose 10 % of points uniformly distributed in the unit cube, a cube of side $0.1^{1/p}$ is needed, which is 0.32 for $p = 2$, 0.63 for $p = 5$ and 0.79 for $p = 10$ — the "neighbourhood" spans most of each axis. The cell below simulates the concentration of distances.

# Distance concentration: ratio of the farthest to the nearest neighbour distance as the dimension grows (uniform data).
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dims = [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000]
n_pts, n_queries = 500, 50
ratio = np.zeros((len(dims), n_queries)); rel_contrast = np.zeros(len(dims))
for i, p in enumerate(dims):
    pts = rng.random((n_pts, p)); qs = rng.random((n_queries, p))
    dmat = np.sqrt(((qs[:, None, :] - pts[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2))      # (queries, points)
    ratio[i] = dmat.max(1) / dmat.min(1)
    rel_contrast[i] = np.mean((dmat.max(1) - dmat.min(1)) / dmat.min(1))
summary = pd.DataFrame({"p": dims, "median farthest/nearest": np.median(ratio, 1).round(2),
                        "mean (max - min)/min": rel_contrast.round(3), "side of cube holding 10 % of data": (0.1 ** (1 / np.array(dims))).round(2)})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.plot(dims, np.median(ratio, 1), "o-", color=BLUE); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("number of dimensions p"); ax.set_ylabel("farthest / nearest distance\n(median over 50 queries)")
ax.set_title("Distance concentration: 'nearest' loses its meaning as p grows"); fig.tight_layout()
summary.set_index("p").T
p 1 2 3 5 10 20 50 100 200 500 1000
median farthest/nearest 1007.87 40.810 19.260 6.930 3.280 2.190 1.600 1.400 1.260 1.160 1.110
mean (max - min)/min 141122.70 60.377 21.032 6.428 2.353 1.218 0.612 0.401 0.266 0.162 0.112
side of cube holding 10 % of data 0.10 0.320 0.460 0.630 0.790 0.890 0.950 0.980 0.990 1.000 1.000

Figure 12. Median ratio of the farthest to the nearest distance among 500 uniformly distributed points, as a function of the dimension. In one dimension the farthest point is about a thousand times farther than the nearest, in two dimensions about forty times; by $p = 100$ the ratio is below 1.5 and by $p = 1000$ the farthest neighbour is barely 10 % farther than the nearest (printed table). The last row of the table gives the side of the cube needed to enclose 10 % of the data. Real data are not uniform — they lie near lower-dimensional structures, which is why k-NN works at all with 30 or 64 features — but the warning stands: with thousands of features (gene expression, spectra), k-NN needs either feature selection or a learned distance.

6.6 Weighted k-NN and k-NN regression

Two extensions are routine. Distance weighting lets each neighbour vote with a weight that decreases with its distance, typically $1/d$, so that a close neighbour counts more than a distant one; Dudani introduced the idea in 1976 and it reduces the sensitivity to the exact value of $k$.[18] k-NN regression predicts a continuous target by the (weighted) mean of the neighbours' targets; it is the simplest non-parametric regression method, and Altman's exposition of it alongside kernel regression is the standard introduction.[19] The cell below applies both to the diabetes data of Unit 2 — 442 patients, 10 baseline variables and a quantitative measure of disease progression one year later[35] — and compares the cross-validated $R^2$ with that of the linear regression of Unit 2.

# k-NN regression on the diabetes data (uniform and distance weights) versus linear regression, 5-fold CV R^2.
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
diab = datasets.load_diabetes()
Xdb, ydb = diab.data, diab.target
kf = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
rows = []
for k in (1, 5, 15, 30, 60):
    for w in ("uniform", "distance"):
        r2 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k, weights=w)), Xdb, ydb, cv=kf, scoring="r2")
        rows.append({"k": k, "weights": w, "CV R²": r2.mean().round(3)})
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="k", columns="weights", values="CV R²")
lin = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), Xdb, ydb, cv=kf, scoring="r2").mean()
print(f"linear regression (Unit 2): CV R² = {lin:.3f}")
res

linear regression (Unit 2): CV R² = 0.489
weights distance uniform
k
1 -0.125 -0.125
5 0.383 0.382
15 0.454 0.451
30 0.448 0.443
60 0.426 0.417

The pattern repeats that of classification: $k = 1$ is poor — its $R^2$ is negative, worse than predicting the mean, because it reproduces the noise of a single patient — intermediate $k$ is best, and very large $k$ smooths the prediction toward the global mean. Distance weighting changes little on these data; its effect is largest at large $k$, where down-weighting the distant neighbours partly undoes the over-smoothing. On these data the linear model of Unit 2 is better than any k-NN regressor, which is the common outcome when the true relation is close to linear and the sample is small: a method that assumes nothing needs more data than one that assumes the right thing.

6.7 Computational cost

k-NN inverts the usual cost profile of a classifier. Training is free — the sample is stored — but every prediction requires the distance from the query to all $n$ stored cases, a cost of order $n \times p$ per query, plus the memory to hold the whole sample. A model deployed on a device, or queried millions of times, pays this price at every use. Space-partitioning structures reduce the search: the k-d tree, introduced by Bentley in 1975, recursively splits the sample along coordinate axes so that most of the stored cases can be excluded from a query without computing their distance, giving near-logarithmic query time in low dimensions;[22] the ball tree does the same with nested hyperspheres and degrades more gracefully as $p$ grows. Beyond a few dozen dimensions the trees stop helping — a consequence of the distance concentration of Section 6.5 — and brute force or approximate methods are used. scikit-learn chooses among brute, kd_tree and ball_tree automatically; the cell below times them on the 1,797 × 64 digits.

# Cost profile of k-NN: fitting is instant, prediction is where the time goes; tree structures versus brute force.
import time
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(Xd, yd, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=yd)
rows = []
for algo in ("brute", "kd_tree", "ball_tree"):
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, algorithm=algo)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); knn.fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr); t_fit = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); acc = knn.score(Xd_te, yd_te); t_pred = time.perf_counter() - t0
    rows.append({"algorithm": algo, "fit time (ms)": round(1000 * t_fit, 1), f"predict time for {len(yd_te)} queries (ms)": round(1000 * t_pred, 1), "accuracy": round(acc, 3)})
print(f"stored training sample: {Xd_tr.shape[0]} cases x {Xd_tr.shape[1]} features; each query compares against all of them (brute)")
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("algorithm")

stored training sample: 1257 cases x 64 features; each query compares against all of them (brute)
fit time (ms) predict time for 540 queries (ms) accuracy
algorithm
brute 0.3 2.5 0.98
kd_tree 0.8 25.7 0.98
ball_tree 2.5 20.5 0.98

Fitting takes a few milliseconds whatever the algorithm (the tree variants spend theirs building the tree); prediction for a few hundred queries takes longer than fitting, which is the reverse of every other classifier in this course. In 64 dimensions the trees are actually slower than brute force — the pruning fails because, as Section 6.5 predicts, almost no stored case can be excluded without computing its distance — and their benefit appears only for $p$ below about 20 and large $n$. The exact timings vary from machine to machine and run to run; the ordering of fit against predict does not. Memory-based methods remain valuable in biomedicine where the "training sample" is itself the object of interest — k-NN imputation of missing values in expression matrices, which fills a missing measurement with the average of the most similar profiles, is a standard preprocessing step that you may have used without knowing its name.[23]

Exercise 3

In the validation-curve cell of Section 6.4, change the metric to Manhattan (KNeighborsClassifier(p=1)) and then to distance weighting (weights="distance"). Does the best $k$ change? Does the training curve still reach 1.000 with distance weighting, and why must it?

7. Support Vector Machines

7.1 The maximum-margin idea

Return to the geometric view. A support vector machine is a discriminative classifier that outputs an optimal hyperplane: given labelled training cases, it returns the hyperplane that best separates the classes, and new cases are classified by the side of the hyperplane on which they fall. Data are linearly separable when such a hyperplane exists — a straight line in two dimensions, a plane in three — and non-linearly separable when no hyperplane separates them and a curved boundary is required (Section 7.3 shows how the machine handles the second case). When two classes are linearly separable, infinitely many hyperplanes separate them, and the perceptron of Unit 1 stops at the first one it finds. Vapnik and his collaborators asked which separating hyperplane is best, and answered: the one farthest from the nearest training case of either class — the hyperplane with the maximum margin, where the margin is defined as the perpendicular distance from the hyperplane to the closest training points of either class.[24],[26] The argument is one of robustness: a boundary that passes close to training cases will misclassify new cases that fall slightly beyond them, whereas a boundary with a wide empty corridor on both sides tolerates such perturbations. The cases that lie exactly on the edge of the corridor determine it and are called support vectors; moving any other case, or deleting it, changes nothing.

Write the hyperplane as $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0$ and code the classes as $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$. The signed distance of a point to the hyperplane is $(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$, and scaling $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ so that the nearest points satisfy $|\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b| = 1$ makes the width of the corridor equal to $2 / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$. Maximising the margin is therefore minimising $\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$:

$$\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} \; \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad y_i (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1 \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n.$$ This is the hard-margin support vector machine: a convex quadratic programme with linear constraints, which has a unique solution whenever the data are separable. The constraints say that every case lies on the correct side of the corridor; the objective makes the corridor as wide as possible. In the solution, $\mathbf{w}$ is a weighted sum of the support vectors alone, $\mathbf{w} = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i$ with $\alpha_i > 0$ only for support vectors.

The cell below generates two separable clusters, fits a hard-margin machine (a very large $C$, see Section 7.2), and draws the hyperplane, the margins and the support vectors.

# The maximum-margin hyperplane on separable data: hyperplane, margin corridor and support vectors.
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
Xb, yb = make_blobs(n_samples=60, centers=[[0, 0], [3.5, 3.5]], cluster_std=0.6, random_state=0)
hard = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(Xb, yb)                 # huge C ~ hard margin
w, b = hard.coef_[0], hard.intercept_[0]
print(f"w = {w.round(3)}, b = {b:.3f}, ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, margin width 2/||w|| = {2 / np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}")
print(f"support vectors: {hard.n_support_.sum()} of {len(yb)} cases (per class {hard.n_support_})")
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(Xb[:, 0].min() - 1, Xb[:, 0].max() + 1, 200), np.linspace(Xb[:, 1].min() - 1, Xb[:, 1].max() + 1, 200))
Z = hard.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.4))
ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-1e9, 0, 1e9], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"], alpha=0.8)
ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-1, 0, 1], colors="k", linestyles=["--", "-", "--"], linewidths=[1, 1.5, 1])
ax.scatter(*Xb[yb == 0].T, color=ORANGE, s=25, label="class −1"); ax.scatter(*Xb[yb == 1].T, color=BLUE, s=25, label="class +1")
ax.scatter(*hard.support_vectors_.T, s=140, facecolor="none", edgecolor=GREEN, lw=2, label="support vectors")
ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Maximum-margin hyperplane (solid) and margins (dashed)"); fig.tight_layout()

w = [0.619 0.445], b = -1.962, ||w|| = 0.763, margin width 2/||w|| = 2.623
support vectors: 3 of 60 cases (per class [2 1])

Figure 13. Sixty separable points, the maximum-margin hyperplane (solid) and the two margin lines (dashed) at signed distance ± 1. The circled points are the support vectors: they lie exactly on the margin lines, and the hyperplane is determined by them alone. The printed margin width $2 / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert$ is the width of the corridor. Every other point could be moved anywhere on its own side of the corridor without changing the solution — the solution is sparse in the data, which is the property that gives the method its name.

7.2 The soft margin and the parameter C

Real classes overlap, and the hard-margin problem then has no solution. Cortes and Vapnik's 1995 formulation introduced slack variables $\xi_i \geq 0$ that measure by how much each case violates the margin, and a parameter $C$ that prices the violations:[25]

$$\min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad y_i (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i, \quad \xi_i \geq 0.$$ A case with $\xi_i = 0$ is on the correct side of its margin; $0 < \xi_i < 1$ means inside the corridor but correctly classified; $\xi_i > 1$ means misclassified. $C$ trades margin width against training violations. A large $C$ punishes every violation: fewer training cases are misclassified, the margin becomes smaller, and the boundary bends to the training cases — a risk of overfitting (low bias, high variance). A small $C$ tolerates violations in exchange for a larger margin: the boundary is more general and more stable, at the risk of underfitting (high bias, low variance). The support vectors are now all cases on or inside the margin, or misclassified.

$C$ is the regularisation parameter of the support vector machine, the inverse of the $\lambda$ of ridge regression in Unit 2, and like $k$ in k-NN it is chosen by cross-validation. The cell below fits linear machines with $C = 0.01$, $1$ and $100$ to the two-feature breast-cancer problem; because the margin is measured in the units of the features, the features are standardised first.

# The effect of C on a linear soft-margin SVM (two standardised features): margin width, support vectors, accuracy.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, C in zip(axes, (0.01, 1, 100)):
    svm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=C)).fit(X2_tr, y_tr)
    plot_regions(ax, svm, X2_tr, y_tr, f"C = {C}: {svm[-1].n_support_.sum()} support vectors\ntrain {svm.score(X2_tr, y_tr):.3f}, test {svm.score(X2_te, y_te):.3f}")
    # draw the margin lines in the original units via the decision function
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(6, 30, 250), np.linspace(-1, 22, 250))
    Z = svm.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
    ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-1, 0, 1], colors="k", linestyles=["--", "-", "--"], linewidths=[0.8, 1.3, 0.8])
    if ax is not axes[0]: ax.set_ylabel("")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 14. Linear soft-margin machines with $C = 0.01$, $1$ and $100$ on the standardised two-feature problem; solid line, the boundary; dashed lines, the margins. With $C = 0.01$ the margin is enormous — it spans most of the data — and almost every case is a support vector; with $C = 1$ and $C = 100$ the corridor is narrow, only the cases in the overlap support it, and the two solutions are almost identical, because once $C$ is large enough that violations are expensive, the same few overlapping cases determine the boundary. The test accuracies in the titles differ little on this easy problem, which is itself a lesson: $C$ matters most where the classes overlap heavily or the sample is small.

7.3 The kernel trick

A linear boundary cannot separate classes arranged in concentric rings or interleaved crescents. The remedy that makes the support vector machine general is the observation, due to Boser, Guyon and Vapnik in 1992,[24] that the training problem and the decision function depend on the data only through inner products $\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j$. If the data are first mapped into a higher-dimensional space by some $\phi(\mathbf{x})$ — adding squares and products of the features, say — a linear boundary there is a curved boundary in the original space, and the inner products become $\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top \phi(\mathbf{x}_j)$. A kernel is a function $K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ that computes this inner product directly, without ever constructing $\phi$; Mercer's theorem of 1909 characterises the functions for which such a $\phi$ exists.[27] The decision function becomes

$$f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i \in \text{SV}} \alpha_i y_i K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) + b,$$

a weighted sum of similarities between the new case and the support vectors. The common kernels are the linear kernel $K = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j$ (the original machine), the polynomial kernel $K = (\gamma\, \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j + r)^d$, whose implicit $\phi$ contains all monomials up to degree $d$, and the radial basis function (RBF) or Gaussian kernel

$$K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \exp\!\big(-\gamma\, \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert^2\big),$$

whose implicit feature space is infinite-dimensional and whose decision function is a sum of Gaussian bumps centred on the support vectors. A fourth kernel sometimes offered, the sigmoid kernel $K = \tanh(\gamma\, \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j + r)$, makes the decision function resemble a two-layer neural network — a sum of sigmoid units centred on the support vectors — which is why it is described as mimicking a neural network; it is not a valid Mercer kernel for all parameter values and is rarely the best choice in practice. Schölkopf and Smola's monograph is the standard treatment of kernel methods;[28] the cell below shows the three kernels on the two classical non-linear problems.

# Linear, polynomial and RBF kernels on two non-linearly separable problems (moons and circles).
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, make_circles
problems = [("moons", *make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.25, random_state=0)),
            ("circles", *make_circles(n_samples=300, noise=0.1, factor=0.4, random_state=0))]
kernels = [("linear", SVC(kernel="linear", C=1)), ("polynomial, degree 3", SVC(kernel="poly", degree=3, C=1)),
           ("RBF, gamma = 1", SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=1, C=1)), ("sigmoid", SVC(kernel="sigmoid", gamma=0.5, coef0=0, C=1))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(9.5, 4.8))
for i, (pname, Xp, yp) in enumerate(problems):
    Xp_tr, Xp_te, yp_tr, yp_te = train_test_split(Xp, yp, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=yp)
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(Xp[:, 0].min() - .4, Xp[:, 0].max() + .4, 200), np.linspace(Xp[:, 1].min() - .4, Xp[:, 1].max() + .4, 200))
    for j, (kname, clf) in enumerate(kernels):
        clf.fit(Xp_tr, yp_tr); ax = axes[i, j]
        Z = clf.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
        ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-1e9, 0, 1e9], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"], alpha=0.8)
        ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, levels=[0], colors="k", linewidths=1.2)
        ax.scatter(*Xp_tr[yp_tr == 0].T, color=ORANGE, s=8); ax.scatter(*Xp_tr[yp_tr == 1].T, color=BLUE, s=8)
        ax.set_title(f"{pname}, {kname}\ntest accuracy {clf.score(Xp_te, yp_te):.2f}", fontsize=8.5); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 15. Two non-linear problems (rows) and four kernels (columns), with the training points and the decision boundary. The linear kernel cannot do better than a straight cut through either problem; the cubic polynomial separates the moons well but describes the rings poorly; the RBF kernel separates both to high accuracy (values in the titles); the sigmoid kernel, whose decision function resembles a small neural network, produces a boundary of its own shape and does not separate either problem well with these parameters, which is representative of its reputation. The RBF kernel is the default of scikit-learn's SVC and of LIBSVM, the library that implements it,[33] and is the usual first choice when nothing is known about the shape of the boundary.

Why a non-linear map makes a non-linear problem linear can be seen without any kernel, with the "lifting" picture of the lecture slides. The rings of Figure 15 are not linearly separable in the plane $(x_1, x_2)$. Add a third feature computed from the first two, $z = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ — the squared distance from the centre — and every point is lifted to a height proportional to that distance: the inner disc stays low, the outer ring rises, and a horizontal plane $z = r^2$ separates them. The cell below performs the lifting explicitly and fits a linear machine in the three-dimensional space.

# Lifting a non-linearly separable problem into a space where it is linearly separable: add z = x1^2 + x2^2.
Xc, yc = problems[1][1], problems[1][2]
z = (Xc ** 2).sum(axis=1)                                        # the new feature: squared radius
X3 = np.c_[Xc, z]                                                # (x1, x2, z)
lin2 = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1).fit(Xc, yc); lin3 = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1).fit(X3, yc)
print(f"linear SVM training accuracy: in (x1, x2) = {lin2.score(Xc, yc):.3f} | in (x1, x2, z) = {lin3.score(X3, yc):.3f}")
w3, b3 = lin3.coef_[0], lin3.intercept_[0]
z_cut = -b3 / w3[2]                                              # height of the separating plane at x1 = x2 = 0
print(f"separating plane: {w3[0]:.2f} x1 + {w3[1]:.2f} x2 + {w3[2]:.2f} z + {b3:.2f} = 0, i.e. approximately z = {z_cut:.2f}")
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
ax0 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1); ax1 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2, projection="3d")
ax0.scatter(*Xc[yc == 0].T, color=ORANGE, s=10, label="outer ring"); ax0.scatter(*Xc[yc == 1].T, color=BLUE, s=10, label="inner disc")
ax0.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax0.set_ylabel("$x_2$"); ax0.set_aspect("equal"); ax0.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax0.set_title("Original plane: not linearly separable")
ax1.scatter(Xc[yc == 0, 0], Xc[yc == 0, 1], z[yc == 0], color=ORANGE, s=8); ax1.scatter(Xc[yc == 1, 0], Xc[yc == 1, 1], z[yc == 1], color=BLUE, s=8)
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.2, 1.2, 8), np.linspace(-1.2, 1.2, 8))
ax1.plot_surface(gx, gy, -(w3[0] * gx + w3[1] * gy + b3) / w3[2], alpha=0.3, color=GREEN)
ax1.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax1.set_ylabel("$x_2$"); ax1.set_zlabel("$z = x_1^2 + x_2^2$", labelpad=2); ax1.view_init(elev=12, azim=-60)
ax1.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88); ax1.set_title("Lifted to 3-D: a plane separates the classes")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.07, right=0.93, bottom=0.12, top=0.9, wspace=0.05)

linear SVM training accuracy: in (x1, x2) = 0.573 | in (x1, x2, z) = 1.000
separating plane: -0.05 x1 + -0.02 x2 + -4.52 z + 2.36 = 0, i.e. approximately z = 0.52

Figure 16. Left: the rings in their original coordinates, where a linear machine is little better than chance (training accuracy printed above). Right: the same points after adding $z = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ as a third feature; the inner disc lies at low $z$, the outer ring at high $z$, and the green plane found by a linear support vector machine in three dimensions separates them perfectly. Projected back onto the original plane, that plane is a circle. The kernel trick achieves the same result for maps that are too large to write out — the RBF map is infinite-dimensional — by computing only inner products.

7.4 Gamma, and the two knobs of an RBF machine

The RBF kernel has a width parameter, $\gamma$. A small $\gamma$ makes each Gaussian bump wide, so that even far-away training points influence the decision at a given location and the boundary is smooth, approaching a linear one. A large $\gamma$ makes the bumps narrow, so that only nearby training points matter and the boundary becomes complex, following individual cases. Together $C$ and $\gamma$ control the complexity of an RBF machine, and both must be tuned by cross-validation, typically over a logarithmic grid — the practical guide distributed with LIBSVM recommends exactly this procedure, preceded by scaling.[33] The cell below draws the decision boundary for every combination of three values of $C$ and three values of $\gamma$ on the moons.

# A grid of decision boundaries: C (rows) x gamma (columns) for the RBF kernel on the moons.
Xm, ym = problems[0][1], problems[0][2]
Xm_tr, Xm_te, ym_tr, ym_te = train_test_split(Xm, ym, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=ym)
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(Xm[:, 0].min() - .4, Xm[:, 0].max() + .4, 150), np.linspace(Xm[:, 1].min() - .4, Xm[:, 1].max() + .4, 150))
Cs, gammas = (0.1, 1, 100), (0.1, 1, 50)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(9.5, 5.0))
for i, C in enumerate(Cs):
    for j, g in enumerate(gammas):
        clf = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=C, gamma=g).fit(Xm_tr, ym_tr); ax = axes[i, j]
        Z = clf.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
        ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, levels=[-1e9, 0, 1e9], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"], alpha=0.8); ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, levels=[0], colors="k", linewidths=1)
        ax.scatter(*Xm_tr[ym_tr == 0].T, color=ORANGE, s=4); ax.scatter(*Xm_tr[ym_tr == 1].T, color=BLUE, s=4)
        ax.set_title(f"C = {C}, gamma = {g}  |  train {clf.score(Xm_tr, ym_tr):.2f}, test {clf.score(Xm_te, ym_te):.2f}, SV {clf.n_support_.sum()}", fontsize=7.2)
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 17. RBF machines on the moons for $C \in \{0.1, 1, 100\}$ (rows) and $\gamma \in \{0.1, 1, 50\}$ (columns); each title gives training and test accuracy and the number of support vectors. Reading across a row, increasing $\gamma$ changes the boundary from nearly straight (small $\gamma$: far points matter, smooth boundary) to a set of islands around individual training cases (large $\gamma$: only nearby points matter, complex boundary). Reading down a column, increasing $C$ narrows the margin and removes training misclassifications at the expense of a more contorted boundary. The two knobs interact: the top-left machine underfits, the bottom-right one memorises — perfect training accuracy, many support vectors, lower test accuracy, the SVM equivalent of $k = 1$ in Figure 11 — and the best test accuracy lies in the interior of the grid. A machine that keeps most of its training cases as support vectors has memorised them, which is a useful warning sign.

7.5 Probabilities, regression and the hinge loss

Probabilities. A support vector machine outputs a signed distance to the boundary, $f(\mathbf{x})$, not a probability. Platt proposed fitting a logistic function $P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = 1 / (1 + \exp(A f(\mathbf{x}) + B))$ to the outputs on held-out data, with $A$ and $B$ fitted by maximum likelihood — Platt scaling;[29] Lin, Lin and Weng later gave a numerically robust fitting procedure, which is what LIBSVM implements; in scikit-learn the same sigmoid calibration is obtained with CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(), method="sigmoid", ensemble=False) (the older SVC(probability=True) interface is deprecated), fitting the two parameters on out-of-fold decision values from an internal 5-fold cross-validation.[30] In a large empirical comparison, Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana found that SVM scores calibrated this way give good probabilities, whereas raw naive Bayes posteriors are among the worst calibrated of all common methods.[31]

Regression. The margin idea transfers to regression by inverting it: support vector regression (SVR) fits a function that stays within a tube of half-width $\varepsilon$ around the targets, penalising only points outside the tube, with the same $C$ and the same kernels; Smola and Schölkopf's tutorial is the reference.[32] The solution is again a sum over support vectors — here the points on or outside the tube.

The hinge loss. Rewriting the soft-margin problem without constraints shows what the machine actually minimises. Since $\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i))$ at the optimum, the problem is

$$\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \max\big(0,\, 1 - y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)\big) + \frac{1}{2C} \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2,$$

a hinge loss on the margin $y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)$ plus an $L_2$ penalty — the same "loss plus regularisation" structure as the logistic regression of Unit 2, whose loss is $\log(1 + e^{-y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)})$. The two losses are compared in the figure below, together with the zero-one loss both approximate. The cell after it demonstrates Platt scaling and SVR on real data.

Figure 18. Loss as a function of the margin $m = y f(\mathbf{x})$. The zero-one loss counts errors and is flat elsewhere, which makes it impossible to optimise by gradient methods. The hinge loss is zero for cases outside the corridor ($m \geq 1$) — these cases exert no force on the solution, which is why only support vectors matter — and grows linearly for cases inside it or misclassified. The logistic loss is never exactly zero: every case, however well classified, keeps pulling the boundary a little, which is why logistic regression has no support vectors and why its coefficients diverge on separable data. Both are convex upper bounds on the zero-one loss, and both penalise confident errors heavily.

# Platt scaling on the breast-cancer SVM, and support vector regression on the diabetes data.
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
svm30 = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
platt = CalibratedClassifierCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1)), method="sigmoid", cv=5, ensemble=False).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
scores, probs = svm30.decision_function(X_te), platt.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
pick = np.argsort(scores)[[0, len(scores) // 4, len(scores) // 2, 3 * len(scores) // 4, -1]]
print("decision function f(x) -> Platt-scaled P(benign | x) for five test cases from most malignant to most benign:")
print(pd.DataFrame({"f(x)": scores[pick].round(2), "P(benign)": probs[pick].round(3), "truth": np.where(y_te[pick] == 1, "benign", "malignant")}).to_string(index=False))

svr_r2 = {C: float(cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVR(kernel="rbf", C=C, epsilon=5)), Xdb, ydb, cv=kf, scoring="r2").mean().round(3))
          for C in (1, 10, 100, 1000)}
print(f"\nSVR (RBF, epsilon = 5) on the diabetes data, CV R² by C: {svr_r2}   | linear regression: {lin:.3f}")

decision function f(x) -> Platt-scaled P(benign | x) for five test cases from most malignant to most benign:
 f(x)  P(benign)     truth
-2.79      0.000 malignant
-1.08      0.011 malignant
 0.98      0.967    benign
 1.70      0.998    benign
 2.44      1.000    benign

SVR (RBF, epsilon = 5) on the diabetes data, CV R² by C: {1: 0.166, 10: 0.466, 100: 0.447, 1000: 0.282}   | linear regression: 0.489

The Platt-scaled probabilities increase monotonically with the decision function and pass through 0.5 near $f(\mathbf{x}) = 0$, turning a distance into a probability that can be thresholded by cost as in Section 3.2. The SVR results show the usual behaviour of a flexible regressor on a small, nearly linear problem: its $R^2$ peaks at an intermediate $C$ (about 0.47 at $C = 10$, close to the 0.49 of the linear model of Unit 2), underfits when $C$ is too small and overfits when it is too large. Support vector machines have been used in medicine since the late 1990s, most influentially for the classification of tumours from gene-expression profiles, where the number of features (thousands of genes) far exceeds the number of patients and a maximum-margin linear classifier with feature selection — Guyon and colleagues' recursive feature elimination — proved both accurate and interpretable.[34] Vapnik's monograph gives the statistical learning theory that explains why margin, rather than dimension, controls the generalisation of such machines.[26]

Key idea

A support vector machine is defined by three choices — the kernel (shape of the boundary), $C$ (tolerance for training violations) and, for the RBF kernel, $\gamma$ (smoothness) — and its solution depends only on the support vectors. The method is not probabilistic, scales poorly beyond some tens of thousands of cases (training is between quadratic and cubic in $n$), and demands feature scaling; in exchange it is among the most accurate off-the-shelf classifiers for small, high-dimensional, noisy problems, which describes most biomedical datasets.

Exercise 4

In the kernel cell of Section 7.3, increase the noise of the moons to 0.4 and refit. Which kernel degrades most? Then set C = 100 for the RBF column and compare training and test accuracy. Explain the result using the slack variables of Section 7.2.

8. Comparing the three families

8.1 An honest comparison on the full data

Every accuracy quoted so far was either a single train–test split or a cross-validation in which the hyper-parameters had been chosen by looking at the same folds. Supplement S1 explains why the second is optimistic: choosing $k$ or $C$ to maximise the cross-validated score and then reporting that score uses the validation data twice. The honest procedure is nested cross-validation — an inner cross-validation inside each training fold chooses the hyper-parameters, and the outer fold, never seen by the inner search, measures performance. The cell below runs it with stratified 5-fold outer folds for the three families, with the logistic regression of Unit 2 as the reference, on all 30 standardised features, and reports the mean ± standard deviation of accuracy and of the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across the outer folds.

# Nested stratified 5-fold cross-validation of the three families (and logistic regression) on all 30 features.
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_validate
inner = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
def tuned(est, grid):
    return GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), est), grid, cv=inner, scoring="roc_auc")
models = {
    "Gaussian naive Bayes":     make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), GaussianNB()),
    "k-NN (k tuned)":           tuned(KNeighborsClassifier(), {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": [3, 5, 9, 15, 25]}),
    "SVM, linear (C tuned)":    tuned(SVC(kernel="linear"), {"svc__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}),
    "SVM, RBF (C, gamma tuned)": tuned(SVC(kernel="rbf"), {"svc__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100], "svc__gamma": [0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1]}),
    "logistic regression (Unit 2)": tuned(LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), {"logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}),
}
rows = []
for name, model in models.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    cvres = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv5, scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc"])
    rows.append({"model": name, "accuracy": f"{cvres['test_accuracy'].mean():.3f} ± {cvres['test_accuracy'].std():.3f}",
                 "AUC": f"{cvres['test_roc_auc'].mean():.3f} ± {cvres['test_roc_auc'].std():.3f}",
                 "wall time (s)": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)})
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
comparison
accuracy AUC wall time (s)
model
Gaussian naive Bayes 0.930 ± 0.012 0.989 ± 0.006 0.0
k-NN (k tuned) 0.960 ± 0.007 0.989 ± 0.008 0.4
SVM, linear (C tuned) 0.975 ± 0.012 0.994 ± 0.005 0.4
SVM, RBF (C, gamma tuned) 0.979 ± 0.013 0.995 ± 0.006 2.3
logistic regression (Unit 2) 0.977 ± 0.012 0.996 ± 0.006 0.5

All five methods classify the Wisconsin data well — every AUC is close to 0.99 — but the accuracies are not all equal, and the honest reading has two parts. The three discriminative methods — the linear and RBF support vector machines and the logistic regression of Unit 2 — reach accuracies around 0.975–0.98 that differ from one another by less than the fold-to-fold standard deviation (about 0.012), so the table gives no grounds for preferring one of them on these data. Naive Bayes, with no hyper-parameter to tune, is the fastest and clearly the least accurate at about 0.93, four to five standard deviations below the discriminative group — the price of its independence assumption on 30 strongly correlated features, consistent with Section 4.5 — although its AUC is almost as high, which confirms that it ranks cases well while mis-stating their probabilities. Tuned k-NN sits in between at about 0.96. The general lesson is typical of small, well-curated, low-dimensional problems: the discriminative methods are indistinguishable, the gap to naive Bayes is real but modest, and the standard deviations across folds — of the order of 0.01 in accuracy — are the resolution below which no claim should be made from a sample of 569 cases. Where the methods differ decisively is in what they offer besides accuracy, and the next subsection tabulates it.

8.2 When to use which

Naive Bayes Bayesian network k-NN SVM
Family generative, probabilistic generative, probabilistic memory-based discriminative, geometric
Main assumption features conditionally independent given the class the dependence structure in the graph near cases share labels; a meaningful distance exists classes separable with a margin in the kernel's feature space
Boundary shape quadratic (Gaussian), linear (equal variances or multinomial) depends on the model arbitrary, local linear or as flexible as the kernel
Needs feature scaling no no yes yes
Hyper-parameters none (smoothing) structure, priors $k$, metric, weighting kernel, $C$, $\gamma$
Outputs probabilities yes, poorly calibrated yes, and full posteriors over any variable by vote fraction, coarse no; Platt scaling needed
Training cost one pass, $O(np)$ counting (known structure); search (unknown) none $O(n^2)$–$O(n^3)$
Prediction cost $O(p)$ inference, exponential in the worst case $O(np)$ per query, memory $O(np)$ $O(\#\text{SV} \cdot p)$
Interpretability per-feature likelihoods, readable high: the graph is the explanation by example ("similar to these patients") linear: coefficients; kernel: low
Sample size works with very few cases small if structure known needs dense sampling; suffers in high $p$ good with small $n$ and large $p$
Handles missing values naturally (skip the feature) naturally (marginalise) needs imputation needs imputation
Typical biomedical use text, baselines, small-sample diagnosis diagnosis and prognosis with expert knowledge imputation, similarity search, small signal problems gene-expression and imaging classification, high-$p$ problems

Three rules of thumb follow. Use naive Bayes as the first baseline on any new problem and as a serious candidate when cases are scarce or features are counts. Use a Bayesian network when the structure of the problem is known and partially observed evidence must be reasoned about — when the question is not only "which class?" but "what is the probability of this finding given those?". Use k-NN when similarity is the natural notion (retrieval, imputation) and the data are dense in a low-dimensional representation; use a support vector machine when the data are high-dimensional, the sample is small, and accuracy matters more than probabilities or explanations. In every case, scale the features when the method is distance-based, put the scaler inside the pipeline, tune hyper-parameters by nested cross-validation, and report the spread across folds.

Bridge to Units 4 and 6

Unit 4 adds a fourth family, decision trees and random forests, which need no scaling, handle mixed data types natively and produce readable rules, and which on tabular biomedical data are often the strongest baseline. Unit 6 shows that a neural network with one hidden layer is also a kernel machine of sorts — it learns its own feature map $\phi$ instead of fixing it in advance — and that the hinge and logistic losses of Figure 18 reappear as its output layer.

9. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • Bayes' theorem as the relation between the forward direction in which test characteristics are measured and the backward direction in which a clinician reasons, and why a positive result of an accurate test for a rare disease (prevalence 1 %, sensitivity and specificity 95 %) leaves a posterior of only about 16 %.
  • The Bayes classifier, the Bayes error as the irreducible error of a problem, and how unequal costs replace the posterior threshold of 1/2 by $\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} / (\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}})$.
  • The conditional-independence assumption of naive Bayes; the three steps (frequency table, likelihood table, posterior) of the categorical hand example; the Gaussian variant's parameters (priors, per-class means and variances) and how its log-posterior is computed; Laplace smoothing and the zero-frequency problem.
  • Why naive Bayes classifies well although its assumption is false (ranking is preserved while probabilities are distorted), and why its posteriors should not be trusted without calibration.
  • A Bayesian network as a DAG plus conditional probability tables, the factorisation of the joint it encodes, inference by enumeration, explaining away, and the three d-separation structures (chain, fork, collider).
  • Naive Bayes as the Bayesian network with one parent; parameter learning as counting; the existence and cost of structure learning.
  • The k-NN rule as a lazy learner, its distance metrics, why feature scaling is mandatory, how $k$ controls the bias–variance trade-off, what the curse of dimensionality does to "nearest", and why prediction rather than training is the expensive step.
  • The maximum-margin hyperplane and support vectors; the soft margin and the meaning of $C$; the kernel trick, the common kernels and the meaning of $\gamma$; Platt scaling; the hinge loss and its relation to the logistic loss.
  • How to compare classifier families honestly (nested cross-validation, mean ± sd across folds) and how to choose among them from their assumptions, scaling needs, costs and interpretability.

10. Self-assessment

1. A test has sensitivity 0.90 and specificity 0.90. Compute by hand the PPV when the prevalence is 2 %, and then when it is 50 %.At 2 %: $P(D \mid T) = (0.9 \times 0.02) / (0.9 \times 0.02 + 0.1 \times 0.98) = 0.018 / 0.116 \approx 0.155$. At 50 %: $0.45 / (0.45 + 0.05) = 0.90$. Only when the prior is 50 % does the PPV equal the sensitivity.
2. In Figure 4, the minimum-risk threshold moved the boundary toward smaller radii. If instead a false positive were five times as costly as a false negative, where would it move and what would the posterior threshold be?The threshold becomes $\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} / (\lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}) = 5/6$: a case is called malignant only when the posterior exceeds 0.83, so the radius threshold moves to larger values and fewer cases are called malignant.
3. In the weather example, compute by hand $P(\text{Yes} \mid \text{Overcast}, \text{Hot}, \text{High}, \text{Windy} = \text{False})$ without smoothing, and explain what happens to the No class.Yes: $9/14 \times 4/9 \times 2/9 \times 3/9 \times 6/9 = 0.6429 \times 0.4444 \times 0.2222 \times 0.3333 \times 0.6667 \approx 0.0141$. No: $5/14 \times 0/5 \times \dots = 0$. The normalised posterior of Yes is exactly 1 because the single zero likelihood $P(\text{Overcast} \mid \text{No}) = 0$ annihilates the whole product for No — the zero-frequency problem that Laplace smoothing prevents.
4. Gaussian naive Bayes with priors 0.5, benign mean (12, 2) and variances (2/3, 2/3), malignant mean (19, 9) and variances (8/3, 8/3). Without computing, say which class the point (12, 2) receives, and which class a point very far from both means receives, and why.(12, 2) is at the benign mean and far from the malignant one: benign. A point very far from both means is assigned to the class with the larger variance (malignant), because the quadratic penalty $(x - \mu)^2 / 2\sigma^2$ grows four times more slowly for the wide class; a narrow Gaussian makes distant points more surprising than a wide one does.
5. Naive Bayes reached 0.94 accuracy with all 30 features although radius, perimeter and area are almost perfectly correlated. Why did the redundancy not hurt the accuracy, and what did it hurt?Under zero-one loss only the ranking of the posteriors matters; counting the same evidence three times inflates both classes' log-likelihoods in a way that rarely changes which is larger (Domingos and Pazzani). What it hurts is calibration: the posteriors are pushed toward 0 and 1, so most test cases receive a posterior above 0.99.
6. In the chest-clinic network, is Smoking independent of X-ray? Is it independent of X-ray given Cancer? Is Cancer independent of Bronchitis given Dyspnoea? Justify each with the graph.No: the chain S → C → X is open, so S and X are dependent. Yes: conditioning on C blocks the chain. No: C → D ← B is a collider; conditioning on D opens the path, making C and B dependent (explaining away) — and the fork C ← S → B is also open unless S is observed.
7. Count the free parameters of the full Asia network (8 binary nodes: Asia, Tuberculosis, Smoking, Cancer, Bronchitis, Either, X-ray, Dyspnoea) given its arrows A → T, S → C, S → B, T → E, C → E, E → X, E → D, B → D.Asia 1, Tuberculosis 2, Smoking 1, Cancer 2, Bronchitis 2, Either 4 (two parents; in the original it is deterministic), X-ray 2, Dyspnoea 4: 18 parameters, against $2^8 - 1 = 255$ for the unrestricted joint.
8. Read the code of the k-NN scaling cell in Section 6.3. Why is the scaler placed inside a make_pipeline with the classifier rather than applied to X before cross_val_score?Inside the pipeline the scaler is fitted on the training folds only within each cross-validation split, so the test fold's mean and variance never influence the model. Scaling X beforehand would use the test cases' statistics — a (mild) form of data leakage that makes the estimate optimistic.
9. Figure 9 shows a training accuracy of exactly 1.000 at $k = 1$. Would this still hold with weights="distance" for any $k$? Would it hold with $k = 1$ if the data contained two identical cases with different labels?With distance weights, the training case itself is at distance 0 and receives infinite weight, so training accuracy is 1.000 for every $k$ (scikit-learn handles the zero distance specially). With duplicated cases of different labels, $k = 1$ cannot classify both correctly, so training accuracy falls below 1.
10. In Figure 13 the maximum-margin hyperplane was supported by very few cases. If one of the non-support cases were moved by a small amount, would the hyperplane change? If a support vector were moved?Moving a non-support case anywhere on its own side of the margin leaves the solution unchanged — it has zero weight $\alpha_i$. Moving a support vector changes the hyperplane, because the solution is determined by the support vectors alone.
11. Explain, in terms of the slack variables and the hinge loss, why an SVM with $C = 100$ on noisy data has more support vectors than one with $C = 1$, as in Figure 17.With a large $C$ the optimiser is unwilling to pay for slack, so it narrows the margin and contorts the boundary (large $\gamma$ allows it) to reduce the violations; many cases end up on or inside the narrow margin, where the hinge loss is active, and all of them become support vectors. With small $C$ a wide margin is accepted, violations are cheap, and the boundary is determined by a smaller set of cases near the middle.
12. Section 8.1 reports accuracies for the two support vector machines and logistic regression that differ by less than the fold-to-fold standard deviation. A colleague proposes to pick the one with the highest mean and report that it is "the best model for breast-cancer diagnosis". What is wrong, and what would you report?A difference smaller than the sampling variability of the estimate is not evidence of a difference; the ranking would likely change with another random split, and selecting the maximum of several noisy estimates is itself optimistically biased. Report all methods with their mean ± sd, state that the three discriminative methods are statistically indistinguishable on 569 cases (while naive Bayes is clearly lower), and choose among the three by the secondary criteria of Section 8.2 (calibration, interpretability, cost), or run a paired test across folds if a decision must be defended.

Glossary

Bayes classifier / Bayes error
The rule that assigns each case to the class of highest posterior probability, optimal when the true distributions are known / its error rate, the irreducible error of the problem.
Bayesian network
A directed acyclic graph over random variables together with a conditional probability table for each node given its parents; it encodes the factorisation of the joint distribution into local conditionals.
Calibration
Agreement between a classifier's predicted probabilities and the observed frequencies: among cases given probability 0.8, about 80 % should belong to the class.
Class-conditional density
$p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c)$, the distribution of the features among the cases of class $c$; the object a generative classifier estimates.
Conditional independence
$A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ when $P(A, B \mid C) = P(A \mid C)\,P(B \mid C)$; the assumption that makes naive Bayes and Bayesian networks tractable.
Curse of dimensionality
The collection of phenomena by which geometric intuition fails as the number of features grows: volume concentrates in corners and shells, and distances between points become nearly equal.
d-separation
A graphical criterion for reading conditional independence off a Bayesian network: two nodes are independent given a set of observed nodes when every path between them is blocked (chains and forks blocked by observing the middle node; colliders blocked unless the collider or a descendant is observed).
Discriminative / generative
A classifier that models $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly (logistic regression, SVM) / one that models $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$ and $P(y)$ and applies Bayes' theorem (naive Bayes, Bayesian networks).
Explaining away
The decrease in the posterior of one cause when another cause of the same observed effect is found to be present; a consequence of conditioning on a collider.
Hinge loss
$\max(0, 1 - y f(\mathbf{x}))$, the loss minimised by the soft-margin SVM; zero for cases outside the margin, linear inside it.
Kernel / kernel trick
A function $K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ equal to the inner product of the two points in some feature space / the substitution of such a function for the inner product in an algorithm, making the algorithm non-linear without constructing the feature space.
k-nearest neighbours (k-NN)
The rule that classifies a case by the majority label (or predicts the mean target) among the $k$ closest training cases under a chosen distance; a lazy learner.
Laplace (additive) smoothing
Adding a pseudo-count $\alpha$ to every cell of a frequency table before estimating probabilities, so that unseen feature values do not receive probability zero.
Lazy learner
A method that builds no model at training time and defers computation to prediction; k-NN is the archetype.
Margin
The perpendicular distance from a separating hyperplane to the closest training cases; the SVM maximises it.
Naive Bayes
The generative classifier that assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class; Gaussian, multinomial, Bernoulli and categorical variants differ in the one-dimensional model of each feature.
Platt scaling
Fitting a logistic function to a classifier's scores on held-out data to convert them into calibrated probabilities; the standard way to obtain probabilities from an SVM.
Posterior / prior / likelihood / evidence
The four terms of Bayes' theorem: $P(\text{class} \mid \text{data})$ / $P(\text{class})$ before the data / $P(\text{data} \mid \text{class})$ / $P(\text{data})$, the normalising constant.
Radial basis function (RBF) kernel
$K = \exp(-\gamma \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert^2)$; the default SVM kernel, whose width is set by $\gamma$.
Soft margin / C
The SVM formulation that allows margin violations measured by slack variables / the parameter that prices them, trading margin width against training errors.
Support vector
A training case that lies on or inside the margin (or is misclassified); the only cases that determine the SVM solution.
Validation curve
A plot of training and cross-validated performance against one hyper-parameter, used to choose its value and to see under- and overfitting.
